Creating custom kernels for the AMD MI300

📅 09 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 32 min read (6407 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~32 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • More than a billion per day: that’s a low estimate of how many requests ChatGPT handles daily, a number which is unlikely to go down soon.
  • But where might that gain come from?
  • It has been revealed that kernels are essential for running operations in neural networks—without a kernel, an operation effectively can't be used.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

More than a billion per day: that’s a low estimate of how many requests ChatGPT handles daily, a number which is unlikely to go down soon. For each request and each generated token, we run an inference of a multi-billion parameters model. This is why model optimization is paramount at each and every level: when one deals with these kinds of scale, even a 1% latency or power gain can bring huge savings.

But where might that gain come from? Model architectures are already well established, and popular models have had quantized weight for a long time now. However, a crucial level at which we can optimize model inference remains: the kernel level. Kernels are the algorithms executed when you do any operation in your network: there are matrix multiplication kernels, convolution kernels, batch normalization kernels, etc. Kernels are low-level, highly-optimized algorithms, often tailored for the device they will be running on. They are notoriously long and hard to write, and require a good understanding of the inner working of the GPU.

It has been revealed that kernels are essential for running operations in neural networks—without a kernel, an operation effectively can't be used. Because of this, new innovations often launch with a "day 0" kernel, typically optimized only for the latest Nvidia hardware. This approach excludes many other devices, particularly AMD GPUs, which, despite offering comparable or superior specs, are often overlooked by kernel developers. Hugging Face collaborated with AMD to deliver state-of-the-art performance on AMD platforms and make it benefit the open source community. As part of this partnership, we decided with AMD to focus on delivering open-source optimized kernels to improve the performance of serving Llama 3.1 405B in FP8 on a node of 8 MI300X using VLLM.

In this blog post, we'll explore how we optimized performance for the MI300X and how each kernel was individually fine-tuned. But first, let’s look at the performance gains achieved using our custom kernels. By combining the following three optimized kernels:.

we achieved significant speedups when running VLLM on a node powered by MI300X GPUs.

Measures were taken with input size 1 and output size 128 to mimic decoding regime. We measure decoding latency using the median over 30 iterations.

Those performance gains were measured in VLLM, but you may also use the kernels separately, as described in the “How to” section that follows.

All kernels described previously are available on the hf-rocm-kernels repository located here. In it, you will find instructions on how to install the package, the source code for each kernels, their respective python bindings, various benchmarking scripts and a test suite. Using benchmarking scripts and a MI300X, you may even reproduce from this blog post. To ensure same results for Torch or VLLM, you can use the same container as we did. You can also use the repo as a base to build your own kernels: it has instructions on how to bind a CUDA-style kernel to python and a simple sample kernel. You may even have a look at branches under development for upcoming kernels, like a compute-and-communicate kernel as described here.

The kernels described will soon be integrated in the AMD fork of the VLLM project, but if you want to have a look at how you might do something like that yourself, you may check out this branch and this document.

We are first going to do a quick refresher on the architecture of the device we are working on: the MI300X. Then, we are going to take a look at the state of our model’s inference before optimizing it. This will allow us to identify bottlenecks and know which custom kernels we need to write. Then, we will take a look at each kernel we have written, which will give us an opportunity to explore how kernel optimization is conducted through many angles.

Before we dive into optimizing GPU code, we need to know how a GPU works. There are a lot of resources out there that already do a great job of explaining the inner workings of your GPU, which I will link right here, here and here. We are still going to run through the different levels of the GPU, as a quick refresher. If you want to skip the refresher and get directly into the details of our custom kernels, click here!

The smallest unit of work in the GPU is the thread. Any time any work is done on a GPU, it’s because a thread executed an instruction. Instructions are basic operations like additions, multiplication, conversion from one data type to another, or loads and stores. Each thread has its own memory, called registers (or VGPRs), which only it can access. A thread can have a maximum of 256 registers, each 32-bit wide. Below is represented a thread with access to its 256 VGPRs.

Threads, except when using load or store instructions, can only execute instructions on their own registers. For instance, to add two vectors A and B together, each thread is going to 1) load in its registers an element from A and 2) another from B, then 3) perform the addition and store the result in another register, and finally 4) store the value from that register in memory. That’s a total of 4 instructions.

The next unit of work is a warp: each warp is composed of 64 threads. Warps don’t have their own memory, but they are of interest to us because all threads in a warp must execute the same instruction at the same time. This is both a guarantee and a constraint.

Warps also allow for different threads to exchange information coming from their registers with other threads in the same warp. Although different threads in a warp have access to different data, the fact that they all have to execute the same instructions means that when writing a kernel, warp-level behavior is what you need to think about.

Warps are bundled together into thread blocks: thread blocks are software abstractions, but run on a hardware component called a compute unit (CU). A single compute unit can run multiple thread blocks at once, but it can only fit 16 warps. Each compute unit has a dedicated L1 cache and shared memory. L1 cache cannot be controlled or allocated and helps with data reuse of all warps situated on the CU. Conversely, shared memory can be allocated and used as a storage shared by all warps. For instance, when we want all warps (and thus threads) in a compute unit to access the same buffer, we allocate it in shared memory. Both shared memory and L1 cache are fast to access because they are “close” to the threads.

In a recent development, thread blocks also offer the ability to synchronize all threads running inside: this is quite useful when dealing with operations that impact shared memory, like initializing an array in shared memory to zero or reduction operations. In general, when writing a kernel, thread blocks are the highest level to take into consideration: it’s very hard to synchronize different thread blocks or make them interact in any way whatsoever. Kernel throughput is tightly linked to the number of compute unit present on the GPU: the more CUs there are, the more thread blocks can be run at the same time, which increases throughput if you manage to use all CUs.

Compute units are then grouped into accelerator complex dies (XCDs), which hold 38 compute units each. Although CUs may not interact with each others, they all share a L2 cache which you can’t control but still may prove useful when re-using data. For instance, when accessing memory, having two compute units located on the same XCD access the same data will reduce loading latency by a lot. L2 cache is quite large: it has a size of 4MB, while shared memory has a size of 64kB and L1 cache contains 32kB.

By assembling 8 XCDs (which gives us 8 * 38 = 304 CUs) and adding a last level of cache (called infinity cache, with 256MB) and a huge quantity of video ram (192GB) we get the MI300X.

In a recent development, all XCDs, and thus all threads, have access to the VRAM, but getting there is quite slow. As you get further away from thread-level, memory becomes slower to access but has a larger size and larger scope, meaning it serves more threads. When optimizing a kernel, there is always a balance to strike between doing lots of operations or loading lots of data, but in general, you want to access the VRAM (commonly referred to as global memory) as little as possible.

Industry observers note that when looking at this figure, we can see why GPUs are referred to as “massively parallel”: here, we have 304 compute units, which can each run 16 warps, each with 64 threads. This means that we can have up to 311296 threads running at the same time, each executing an instruction of its own. Keep in mind an instruction is something basic like an addition, so simple routines like Newton’s method can be quite long to run for a single thread. GPUs are not optimized for instructions to run fast, i.e. for the latency of each instruction to be low: that would be a latency-oriented device. They are optimized for many threads to be run together, consuming and outputting a large quantity of data: it is a throughput-oriented device. When optimizing a kernel for the GPU, we adapt in consequence: it is better to have an algorithm running a few instructions on many threads at once, than having it run many instructions on a few threads. Hence calling algorithms running on GPUs “parallel”.

What can get in the way of such algorithms running in an optimized manner are three things: when there is a lot of data to load (memory bound), when there are many operations to performs (compute bound) or when threads have to work together (synchronization overhead).

Recent findings suggest that when optimizing a workload, the first thing to do before writing a single line of code is to profile the current state of the workload. In our case, we are going to profile the model inference in VLLM to get an idea of how much time each operation is taking up. This can help identify major bottlenecks and which kernels we can tackle first for maximum speedup. For instance, here is the breakdown for batch size 32:.

We can see the different parts of the network through each slice:.

Already we can see that most of the latency comes from GEMMs and communications, but also that attention and the operations surrounding it are not a major contributor to latency. This can come as a surprise, because a lot of papers focus on attention and reducing its cost, but it seems that through a combination of KV caching and FlashAttention, which has already been optimized in VLLM, this part may no longer be a top priority. Surprisingly, the two calls made to the “RMS norm” kernel are quite costly, so there might be a large benefit to optimizing that kernel. Along with the SwiGLU kernel, they represent 15% of the total latency, which is not negligible. All in all, working on those two kernels, plus trying to gain a small speedup on GEMMs may be our best course of action. To check that this performance breakdown is not a fluke, we can take a look at other batch sizes:.

Sources indicate that we can see the pattern that emerged for batch size 32 holds up for other batch sizes, albeit with the latency contribution of GEMMs and communications becoming greater as the batch size increases. Also, it seems that batch size 32 is an outlier when it comes to the latency of GEMMs: it’s probably because the GEMMs chosen when batch size is 32 have been manually tuned or because batch size 32 presents good memory alignment patterns, so GEMMs for batch size 32 are faster than for batch size 24 or 28.

Now that we have identified some hot spots to optimize, let’s take a look at the first kernel we wrote: the RMS norm kernel.

According to recent reports, in each decoder block, we have two main parts: an attention block and an MLP block. Both begin with a residual connection between two inputs: the current hidden states x x x and the residual r r r . Both have the same shape, which is n n n rows (as many as there are tokens) and d d d columns. After they are added together, we apply a row-wise Root Mean Square (RMS) norm to x x x and, since the model is in FP8, we quantize x x x to FP8 using a scale s s s . Simply fusing those three operations into a single kernel can deliver a nice performance boost. Mathematically, the operations we have to perform are the following:.

i+j+kx←x+rr←xV=∑i=1dxi2x←xV+ϵxQ=Qfp8(s∗x∗w) \begin{align} \phantom{i + j + k} &\begin{aligned} x &\leftarrow x + r\\ r &\leftarrow x \end{aligned}\\ &\begin{aligned} V &= \sum_{i=1}^{d} x_i^2 \end{aligned}\\ &\begin{aligned} x &\leftarrow \frac{x}{\sqrt{V + \epsilon}} \\ x_Q &= Q_{\text{fp8}} \left( s * x * w\right) \end{aligned} \end{align} i+j+k​xr​←x+r←x​V​=i=1∑d​xi2​​xxQ​​←V+ϵ​x​=Qfp8​(s∗x∗w)​​​.

where w w w is a d d d -sized weight vector. Steps (1) and (3) are pretty basic. For step (1), we just need to position each thread to a different location in the tensor, load some elements of x x x and r r r , add them and store back r r r . For step (3), each thread performs some scalar operations (addition, square root, division) and a conversion to FP8. All of this, each thread can do on its own: this is perfectly suited to the parallel nature of the GPU. The step to watch out for is (2): we need to sum over d d d , which means either each thread is going to visit each of the d d d columns, or we need to exchange data between threads. The greater d d d is, the more data we would have to load for the first option, so the less viable it becomes. We are going to pick the second option: synchronize threads at the block level, and they will exchange data using the shared memory. Each thread is going to accumulate a part of V V V on its own and then we are going to sum all of those parts across the thread block, which is what we call a reduction. Since V V V is computed across an entire row, we are going to assign a thread block for each row.

When compared to out-of-the-box pytorch, the bare bones version of this kernel brings about a 10x speedup. But this is not enough: there are still many optimizations we can add on top of this.

In terms of latency, one of the most costly operation is accessing VRAM, also called global memory. Luckily, there are some easy-to-follow principles that can dramatically reduce the cost of loading data.

First, we can take a look at how much data a single thread can load in a single instruction: using the MI300X instruction guide, we see that the largest load we can make from global memory is 128 bits wide. Since we are loading FP16 data, we are going to load 128b / 16b = 8 elements per load. For fp32 elements, it would correspond to 4 elements per load.

Secondly, we make sure memory accesses are coalesced. Since each thread is part of a warp, when one thread reaches a “load” instruction, all other threads in the warp do too. For efficiency’s sake, these “load” instructions are then bundled together across the warp. The warp then collectively fetches the data needed and each thread gets the data it requires. Maximum efficiency is reached when the warp fetches a single chunk of data without any gap in it: this is what we call contiguous data. An problem arises when we need to load more data that can be loaded in one “load” instruction, and is illustrated below.

In a recent development, in this hypothetical scenario, we have two threads in the same warp. They need to collectively load 16 fp32 elements, without constraint on which thread loads which element. This is a typical “reduction” situation. Since a thread can only load 4 fp32 elements per instruction, we have at least two ways of reading the data, represented in scenario (a) and (b). To decide which scenario is best, we need to look at this from warp perspective, not thread perspective. In scenario (a), the first load fetches elements 0,1,2,3,8,9,10,11 : we see that the data is not contiguous, because there is a gap between elements 3 and 8. While in scenario (b), the first load fetches elements 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7 : we load contiguous data. Same goes for the second load. Thus scenario (b) is better. Although in scenario (a) we end up with 8 contiguous elements per thread, this does not matter: what matters is whether or not the warp loads contiguous data. This matters because if the warp can only load 8 contiguous elements in one cycle, then each load of scenario (a) is processed in two cycles, while in scenario (b), each load only needs the one cycle.

Sources indicate that third, we reduce the number of stores: when we look at steps (1) and (3) we can see that there are only two stores needed: one for r r r and one for xQ x_Q xQ​ . After step (1) we can already store r r r and be done with that. But we still need to access the modified version of x x x after step (2) is done. To do that, we can store the modified version of x x x in global memory and reload it after step (2) is done and rely on cache hits when reloading it. Or, if x x x is small enough, we can store its modified version in shared memory: if x x x is in FP16 and we only have one thread block per CU, then we can store 64KB / 2B = 32 * 1024 elements in shared memory per thread block. In the case of Llama 405B, d d d is equal to 16384, so that fits. Using shared memory provides a nice speedup over relying on cache hits, especially when many thread blocks are active at once: if the L1 cache is not big enough to fit the whole of x x x, then we have to rely on L2 cache, which is shared by 38 CUs.

Apart from memory access, we can also optimize computational efficiency, but we are going to leave that for the next kernel, as they will be similar in both cases.

When we apply the optimizations discussed above, we get the following results:.

In a recent development, with a [X, 16384] shaped FP16 input tensor. The most basic version of our kernel, referred to as “Pointwise”, has no memory-related optimization and already reveals at least a x4 speedup over torch. It is less optimal than VLLM’s implementation of the kernel, but our “Vectorized” implementation beats both “Pointwise” and VLLM. This is the version of the kernel that implements coalesced 128 bits loads, which is only surpassed by the “Vectorized + SMEM” (SMEM stands for shared memory) implementation, that offers a notably better speedup ratio than VLLM for both low and high batch sizes.

Sources indicate that in the MLP block, after the kernel we have just written about, comes a projection which we have referred up to this point as “Gate / Up” projection. The reason we call it that way is because the “Gate / Up” projection is actually a concatenation of two projections with the same input: “Gate” and “Up”. Thus, we will write the result x x x of the “Gate / Up” projection as x=xG∣xU x = x_G | x_U x=xG​∣xU​ where ∣ | ∣ is the concatenation operator applied along the column axis. xG x_G xG​ and xU x_U xU​ have the same dimensions. The reason we need those two projections is the SwiGLU activation function that comes right after, which results y y y is defined by equation (4). The SwiGLU activation function is followed by the “Down” projection, which in our case is in FP8, so we also need to quantize y y y as shown in equation (5):.

i+j+ky=σ(xG)⋅xUyQ=QFP8(s∗y) \begin{align} \phantom{i + j + k}& \begin{aligned} y = \sigma \left( x_G \right) \cdot x_U \\\end{aligned}\\ &\begin{aligned} y_Q = Q_\text{FP8} \left( s * y \right) \end{aligned} \end{align} i+j+k​y=σ(xG​)⋅xU​​yQ​=QFP8​(s∗y)​​​.

where σ \sigma σ is the sigmoid function: σ(x)=e−x/(1+x) \sigma (x) = e^{-x} / (1 + x) σ(x)=e−x/(1+x) . We are going to write a fused kernel that takes care of all of this. For this kernel, optimizations described for the RMS kernel are still relevant with the expection of the shared memory buffer. We will focus here on computation-related optimizations.

There are two ways we are going to increase the speed of our kernels: increase the volume of work done for each instruction executed and use faster instructions.

It has been revealed that to increase the amount of work done per instruction, we can use packed instructions. Packed instruction are useful when we want to apply the same operator on several elements: rather than executing one instruction per element, we execute one instruction over a vector of element. In a CPU, packed (or vectorized) instructions are the bread-and-butter of single-threaded optimization, as the AVX family of instruction can attest to. There are a few packed instructions on GPU, but they can be quite useful in the right place. On the MI300X there is, among others, packed instruction for FP16 addition and multiplication, which we will use for both steps. There also exists packed conversion from FP32 to FP8, which can provide a nice boost in performance when compared to non-packed conversion. As a matter of fact, there is no conversion from any other data type than FP32 to FP8, so for the RMS norm kernel and this one, we have to go to FP32 precision in order to convert to FP8.

However this is not an issue in this kernel: the sigmoid function σ \sigma σ require us to compute an exponent, which is an operation that greatly benefits from FP32 precision. And this is in an instance where we can optimize computation by using a faster instruction: instead of using the exp instruction, we scale the input by log(2) \text{log}(2) log(2) and use the exp2 instruction, which is much faster. We suffer an almost negligible loss in precision but also reduce latency.

We get the following table for a [X, 16384] shaped FP16 input tensor:.

With memory and compute optimizations tailored for the MI300X, we get a kernel that is more than 14 times faster than Torch on average and from 27% to 100% faster than VLLM’s kernel.

It has been revealed that as we have seen earlier, about 60% of the model’s inference latency comes from projections, which rely on GEMM kernels. GEMM kernels are heavily optimized in dedicated libraries such as hipBLASLT rocBLAS on AMD, so writing a custom kernel that performs better in all cases is quite hard. But if we focus on some edge cases that are relevant to us, and write a GEMM kernel for those specific cases, then there is a chance our custom kernel may be faster than the ones in the dedicated libraries.

In both prefill and decoding, the input of any of the network’s projection has as many rows as there tokens being processed. And during decoding, the number of tokens being processed is equal to the batch size. So during decoding, the number of input rows of all GEMM kernels is equal to the batch size, which for our purposes ranges between 1 and 256. We are going to take an interest with very low batch sizes. When we have a GEMM A∗B=C A * B = C A∗B=C such that A A A has few rows and many columns, we say that the GEMM is skinny. The reason we have a specific term for such GEMMs is that they are ill-fitted for the classic GEMM algorithm we run on GPU. Usually, the efficiency of GEMM kernels comes from tiling: we divide the result matrix in many sub-matrices, called tiles, and we assign each tile to a different compute unit (CU). If we have many tiles, we can use many CUs and GPU usage is high. This is illustrated in the figure below.

But if the input A A A has very few rows, then only a few tiles can be formed, which results in only a few compute units active, hence low GPU utilization:.

Skinny GEMMs are fundamentally inconvenient for the GPU. In the next part, we are going to see how through a custom kernel that assumes we are in a skinny GEMM context, we can make them more convenient.

Sources indicate that since the main issue of skinny GEMMs is that we use too few compute units, the first thing we can do is figure out a way to use more. To do this, we can exploit the following mind-breaking formula:.

cij=∑k=1Kaikbkj=(∑k=1K/2aikbkj)+(∑k=1+K/2Kaikbkj) c_{ij} = \sum_{k=1}^K a_{ik} b_{kj} = \left( \sum_{k=1}^{K/2} a_{ik} b_{kj} \right) + \left( \sum_{k=1+K/2}^{K} a_{ik} b_{kj} \right) cij​=k=1∑K​aik​bkj​=​k=1∑K/2​aik​bkj​​+​k=1+K/2∑K​aik​bkj​​.

It has been revealed that thanks to the associativity of the sum, we can split the main GEMM along the shared axis (commonly referred to as the K axis) and replace one GEMM with several sub-GEMMs that are executed concurrently. Each sub-GEMM is going to use as many CUs as the main one would have, so the number of CUs used is multiplied by the number of times we split the K axis. This is shown in the figure below:.

It has been revealed that here, we set split K equal to 2 and thus double the amount of CU used at once. Since we get partial results, we need to add them up after the both sub-GEMMs are done. What may seem counter-intuitive is that we are adding an operation, summing the partial results, yet we claim to reduce the latency of the overall process. But since each CU needs to go through the entire K axis to compute the result, because we are cutting it in two, the amount of work done by each CU is also cut in two. If the amount of work saved this way counter balances the amount of work added by the summing up of the final results, then we have an overall optimization. This is generally true as long as K is large and the original GEMM uses less than 50% of the GPU.

According to recent reports, if we assume that through split-K, most compute units are busy with their own tile, we can focus the scope of optimization at the compute unit level. We are going to take a look at how the actual matrix multiplication is done, and how we can accelerate it.

In state of the art GPUs like the MI300X, matrix multiplication is handled by a dedicated hardware unit called tensor cores. Tensor cores only perform matrix multiplications, but they do so at very high speed. The format of tensor core instruction is mfma_MxNxK... where mfma stands for matrix fused multiply-add, M is the number of rows of the left-hand matrix, N the number of column of the right-hand matrix, and K is the shared dimension of both. We illustrate a hypothetical instruction mfma_2x2x4 below:.

There are only a few tensor core instructions, but for any triplet MxNxK using the dedicated tensor core instruction is much faster than any other alternative. Tensor core instruction also come in two flavours: “dense” and “sparse”. Dense instruction correspond to standard matrix multiplication. Sparse instructions assume that the left-hand side matrix A A A has a 4:2 structured sparsity pattern, which means that two out of every 4 elements along the matrix K axis are zero. Mathematically, for any i,j i, j i,j such that ai,4j+3 a_{i, 4j+3} ai,4j+3​ is an element of A A A , we have at least two zeros in (ai,4j,ai,4j+1,ai,4j+2,ai,4j+3) \left( a_{i,4j}, a_{i,4j+1}, a_{i,4j+2}, a_{i,4j+3} \right) (ai,4j​,ai,4j+1​,ai,4j+2​,ai,4j+3​) . Below is an example of a sparse matrix.

Let’s get back to our model, Llama 405B in FP8. For FP8, we only have two dense tensor core instruction: 16x16x32 and 32x32x16 . We also have one sparse instruction of size 16x16x64 . For an input with 8 rows, using even the smallest dense instruction 16x16x32 means that we have to add 8 rows of padding to our input, which is a waste of compute resources. One can wonder if we can use the sparse instruction instead: after all, if half of a 16 rows matrix is 4:2 sparse, we can fully describe its non-zero coefficients using a dense 8 rows matrix. Conversely, if we have an 8 rows dense matrix, we can fit all of its data into a 16 rows matrix with 4:2 sparsity. And the benefit of using the sparse instruction is obvious: the dense instruction has K=32 while the sparse instruction has K=64 . For the same amount of cycles, the sparse instruction has twice the depth. We illustrate this sparsity trick in the figure below with a 1 row input and the 2x2x4 dense instruction and its sparse 2x2x8 counterpart.

Using this trick, we can notably speed up our GEMM for any input with 8 or less rows, which results in a reduction in per-token latency for any decoding batch that has less than 8 requests.

In a recent development, we have seen that in a skinny GEMM, the fact we have a little number of rows limits the number of output tiles, which in turns limit the GPU utilization. But the small number of rows also limits the number of rows each output tiles has, which in turns reduces what we call arithmetic intensity. Simply put, arithmetic intensity is the amount of work done divided by the amount of data loaded to do that work. Let us compare two examples:.

sn=∑i=1nxitn=∑i=1nyi=y (1+tn−1) s_n = \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i \\ t_n = \sum_{i=1}^n y^i = y ~( 1 + t_{n-1}) sn​=i=1∑n​xi​tn​=i=1∑n​yi=y (1+tn−1​).

According to recent reports, where x x x is an n n n -sized vector and y y y is a scalar. To compute sn s_n sn​ , we load n n n elements and perform n−1 n-1 n−1 additions. To compute tn t_n tn​ , we load 1 element and perform 2n−1 2n-1 2n−1 additions and multiplications. So the “arithmetic intensity” of computing sn s_n sn​ is n−1n \frac{n-1}{n} nn−1​ while tn t_n tn​ is 2n−1 2n - 1 2n−1 : the computation of tn t_n tn​ is more “arithmetically intensive” than the computation of sn s_n sn​ . What we see here is that when the lower arithmetic intensity is, the more data we need to load to perform work.

It has been revealed that why does this matter to us? Well, we have seen that loading data from VRAM has a high latency cost, which is not great for the GPU. In other words, workloads with low arithmetic intensity are ill-suited for the GPU, and it turns out skinny GEMMs have lower arithmetic intensity than their non-skinny counterparts. This becomes intuitive when looking at the figure below: we can see that when we divide the amount of data loaded by two, we divide the number of output coefficients by 4, due to the quadratic nature of the GEMM’s dimensions.

In a skinny GEMM the number of rows of the output tile is limited and so is the arithmetic intensity. Already this means that we are going to need to load a lot of data to compute an output tile. Furthermore, since we are using FP8 arithmetic, computation is quite fast, so we cannot rely on computation time to hide the latency of data loading. All in all, it would be ideal to have more threads in charge of loading data than threads in charge of computing the result.

According to recent reports, to achieve this, we are going to use a technique called warp specialization. Instead having all warps in the thread block execute the same instructions, we are going to dedicate some warps to loading data only and some to computing the results only. The warps in charge of loading data are called producers and the ones that compute the results are named consumers. Producers and consumers work asynchronously: producers first load data from the VRAM, which is slow, and make it available to the consumers by storing it in a shared memory buffer. Until data is available in shared memory, the consumer is idle. After it data is made available, the consumer loads it from shared memory, which is fast, and computes the result. Coordination of producers and consumers is achieved through a queue stored in shared memory. When a producer finishes storing data in a shared memory buffer i i i , it changes the state of the i i i th variable of the queue to signal data is available there. The consumer is watching out for this, and begins loading data afterwards. When it is done, it changes the i i i th variable of the queue to signal that data can be written over in buffer i i i . In the figure below, we represent the steps involved in a simple asynchronous GEMM with one producer, one consumer and a queue of size 2.

What makes the whole process work is that once buffer 0 0 0 is filled by a producer, it can start working on buffer 1 1 1 without waiting for the consumer to have loaded the data from buffer 0 0 0. The goal is to have a queue large enough for the producers to be constantly filling buffers and consumers constantly consuming them. The size of queue is constrained by the size of the shared memory.

It has been revealed that we also need to tune the ratio of producers to consumers: we have noted that we have a low arithmetic intensity, so we need to load a lot of data to do a relatively fast computation. Hence, we are going to have a lot of producer warps (typically 8 or 10) for a few consumer warps (something like 2 or 3). Furthermore, we can exploit the fact the GEMM is skinny by having separate producers for the input (the skinny matrix) and the weights (the non-skinny matrix). To make the output tile bigger in the dimension in which it is not constrained in, which is the columns dimension, we allocate more producers for the weights.

For a more in-depth blog post about asynchronous GEMMs, I encourage you to check out this blog post. A lot of its contents are not applicable in our case though: the MI300X has no warp-level barriers, only a single thread block-level barrier. This led to “fun” shenanigans like ASM to ensure warps waited at their barriers, shared memory loads and stores were resolved before checking the barrier state, and careful handling of the modular nature of the queue. All this would be out of place here, but I encourage you to check out the code or ask away in the comments. A deep dive on the details of async handling might be coming in the future.

In a recent development, through warp specialization and asynchronous work, we can adapt our kernel to the low arithmetic intensity workload, but is that enough to come ahead of libraries like hipBLASLT? The answer is yes, in some cases.

It has been revealed that since Torch already binds a highly optimized GEMM taken from AMD’s linear algebra library, we are not going to get speedups in the same range as for the two last kernels. We are first going to take a look at the three GEMM dimension that are of interest to us: namely, the GEMMs dimensions associated with the QKV projection, the Gate / Up projection and the Down projection. The Output projection is being left out because its dimensions do not correspond to the skinny GEMM case.

It has been revealed that measures are taken after 500 warmups iterations, over 2000 profiling iterations, using CUDA graph and multiple weights to avoid cache hits. In order, the GEMM dimensions shown above correspond to QKV projection (N = 2304 and K = 16384), Gate / Up projection (N = 13312 and K = 16384) and Down projection (N= 16384 and K = 6656). We can see that for those dimensions, which have been tuned for, there is a notable speedup for low number of rows (M = 1, 8, 16) but less so for more rows (M = 32). Especially for dimensions in which we can use our sparsity trick (M = 1, 8) we see a notable speedup over Torch, which probably pads everything to 16 rows to use the smallest MFMA instruction.

Recent findings suggest that in this post, we explored just a handful of the many kernel optimization techniques available. If you're interested in experimenting with them, feel free to dive into the hf-rocm-kernels repository and start tinkering! And if you develop a kernel you like of and want to distribute it, be sure to check out kernel-builder and kernels — two Hugging Face packages designed to help kernel builders make their work widely available and more impactful.

In a recent development, great work! For the Skinny GEMM, do you have numbers for % improvements from sparse mfma and warp specialization (WS) separately? Trying to understand what the impact of WS for different shapes, without sparse mfma.

Looking at the code, my understanding is that sparsity is only used for M = 8. Is this correct?

How does the async handling work?

Recent findings suggest that we use an int16 variable in the shared memory (a semaphore), which can be looked up by any warp on the SM. The thing you have to be carefull about is to have all instructions related to SMEM or GMEM finished before changing the state of the semaphore. For instance, you have to explicitly wait for SMEM stores to be over before switching the semaphore.

Sources indicate that eleven days after leaving Nvidia, Jensen Huang is back as president, CEO, and a board director. The board voted unanimously to reinstate him on Monday, saying it was satisfied with his candor and ability to lead following a series of meetings. It also remarked input from senior levels of the US government left it confident that his reinstatement poses no national security risk.

Industry observers note that I didn’t see this coming. Huang was dishonest to the public and to his board. He admitted to having affairs not only with an alleged Chinese spy, but also with an employee who directly reported to him. He is accused of facilitating the sale of Nvidia AI chips to companies like Megaspeed that knowingly purchased them with the intention of smuggling them into China, a contravention of US trade restrictions.

In a recent development, as recently as November 17th, the board chair, Harvey Jones, reiterated that the organization had no intention of bringing back Huang as CEO. But things changed quickly on Sunday as President Trump reportedly reassured the board that Huang’s reinstatement posed no security risk to US intelligence, something that the new Democratic-led Congress will be sure to test via repeated subpoenas in the new year.

As Huang walked into the atrium at Nvidia’s headquarters, staff gathered around to cheer his return, and he addressed the crowd by saying he would be a “better CEO the second time around,” as if 11 days of unemployment had given him sufficient time to evaluate his past behavior.

It has been revealed that nvidia’s stock was up over 30% on Monday, rebounding from a disastrous end to last week that wiped out $4 trillion in Nasdaq value. It’s hard not to see Huang’s return as a direct response to this short-term disruption, which also hinted at a much more serious correction in the stock market. Nvidia’s stock had already fallen 24% between the day Huang resigned and Friday’s crunch, and with looming regulation from Congress in 2027, a rudderless AI industry could have been disastrous for the US economy writ large.

Recent findings suggest that though things may appear to be back to normal, or as normal as possible given the insanity of the past couple of weeks, Huang has returned to a very different trade environment. While he was away, Nvidia’s board formed a National Security and Export Control Committee to investigate whether the tech giant’s actions violated any US embargoes. And as part of Huang’s return, Nvidia has committed to hiring its first chief compliance officer, an executive who will ostensibly not report directly to the CEO.

I was pretty gobsmacked when I saw the news of Huang’s return come across the wire at 9am ET yesterday. I’m still wrapping my head around it. Is Nvidia too massive to fail, or just a symptom of a larger interdependency between the US executive branch and Big Tech? Huang promises to be a better leader this time around, but to whom: his employees, his customers, or his shareholders? Because he appears to be a very different person to each of those groups.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Multiple employees from both OpenAI and Anthropic are sounding the alarm on the AI labs’ latest models. According to Axios, researchers are still looking for ways to contain and control unreleased models as they become more powerful, leading to debates about whether these models should be released publicly or if they should remain for internal use only. Some people are also arguing that it’s becoming impossible to keep the latest AI leashed and that companies should stop their development immediately.

Industry observers note that “If we continue trying to make models much smarter, such that they’re actually smarter than us... they will in fact be able to trick us successfully,” a researcher told the publication. “And once you get to that point, many of the schemes that we’ve had at work up until now sort of go out the window.” There have previously been various incidents where unreleased models were able to break out of their testing environments and hack their way around the internet.

According to recent reports, the report, which claims to have more than two dozen sources, cites "multiple" employees at frontier AI companies who worry their execs will choose profits over safety when it comes to releasing AI models. Furthermore, "they feel executives have become out of touch with the severity of safety risks.".

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has even warned about an even more devastating occurrence, saying that an AI-driven botnet “swarm” could take over the internet in less than a year. The organization went as far as listing “existential risks to humanity” as one of its risk factors in its IPO prospectus, although it has ironically proposed an AI safety bill that only kicks in if 50 deaths or $1 billion in damages are on the line.

Jensen Huang, the CEO of the company behind some of the hardware that enabled these breakthroughs in AI, said that “we have to shut the labs down” if these AI models prove to be unsafe, and that the civil and criminal liabilities that labs and developers would incur if AI models cause damage would be “incredible.” Still, he said that these fears are nothing but a distraction and not a call for regulation. A former OpenAI safety employee also said that the company’s safety culture is inherently broken and is calling for Silicon Valley to rely on safety experts from nuclear engineering and aviation to help “ensure that no single machine failure or human error would result in tragedy.”.

Sources indicate that A few months after the news of AI models escaping their testing environments, the White House convened the United States’ top AI tech executives, where they promised to “self-police” AI development and take steps “to build a positive future.” Despite that, a Democrat congresswoman has called for a ban on artificial superintelligence, echoing Sen. Bernie Sanders’ proposal to put a 20-year prison term on anyone caught developing the technology, and calling artificial intelligence an “out-of-control” industry.

Pose detection in the browser is a solved problem. You can load a model, point it at a webcam, and get a skeleton tracking a human body in real time, on a laptop, with no server involved.

And then you have a skeleton that follows someone around the screen, which is a toy.

Sources indicate that the gap between that toy and a feature someone would pay for is smaller than most developers expect, and it isn't made of machine learning. It's made of trigonometry you already know. This article builds a working bicep-curl rep counter to show exactly where that line falls — and more importantly, which side of it your bugs live on.

According to recent reports, I'm using MediaPipe Pose Landmarker from Google AI Edge, which is Apache-2.0 licensed and runs entirely in the tab. Here's the whole setup:.

It has been revealed that point that at a element carrying a camera stream and call detectForVideo. What comes back, per frame, is this:.

Thirty-three points. Each one is a normalised coordinate — x and y run 0 to 1 across the frame, z is a relative depth estimate — plus a visibility score saying how confident the model is that it can actually see that joint.

That's the entire output. Coordinates and confidences.

The model has no concept of exercise. It doesn't know what an arm is for. It has never heard of a bicep curl. It reports where it thinks your joints are, thirty-odd times a second, and stops.

Everything that turns that into a product is yours, and it's ordinary code.

Recent findings suggest that A bicep curl is a change in the angle at the elbow. The elbow angle is defined by three of those 33 points: shoulder, elbow, wrist. In MediaPipe's pose topology those are indices 11, 13 and 15 on the left side, 12, 14 and 16 on the right.

Getting the angle is two vectors and a dot product:.

In a recent development, this is the same maths you'd use to point a game character in a direction. Nothing about it is machine learning, and that matters for a reason I'll come back to.

In a recent development, one thing to notice: I'm ignoring z entirely. The depth estimate is relative, not metric — it's good enough for working out which parts of a body are nearer the camera, and not good enough to measure anything. For a 2D elbow angle, using it adds noise and buys nothing.

Here's where almost everyone's first attempt breaks.

The naive version looks at the angle and counts whenever the arm is up:.

It has been revealed that run that at 30 frames a second and one slow curl gives you about twenty reps. You haven't counted repetitions. You've counted frames in which the arm happened to be bent.

Sources indicate that A rep isn't a state. It's a transition between states:.

It has been revealed that fifteen lines, and that's the feature. The counter increments exactly once per cycle, on the edge, because the guard on phase makes every other frame in that cycle a no-op.

If you used a single threshold — say, 100 degrees — you'd get a counter that fires repeatedly whenever someone holds their arm near 100 degrees and the estimate jitters by a degree either side. Every tiny fluctuation across the line is a transition, and every transition is a rep.

Sources indicate that two widely separated thresholds give you hysteresis. Once the arm is "up," it has to travel all the way past 150 degrees before the counter will consider another rep. Noise of a few degrees can't produce a count because no amount of jitter near 55 crosses 150.

Recent findings suggest that this is the same trick a thermostat uses to avoid switching the heating on and off every few seconds, and it's the single most useful pattern in this whole category of work. Any time you turn a continuous signal into discrete events, you want two thresholds, not one.

visibility is the field people skip, and skipping it is how you get phantom reps.

When a joint goes out of frame or gets occluded, the model still returns a coordinate for it. It is obliged to return 33 points. What it does is return a guess, with a low visibility score attached — and a guessed wrist position can swing wildly between frames, which looks exactly like a very fast curl.

Returning null and having enhancement bail out means an occluded frame holds the current state rather than corrupting it. The arm stays "up" until the model can actually see it come down.

If you want to be stricter, smooth the angle over the last three or four frames with a rolling median before it reaches the state machine. A median rejects single-frame outliers in a way a mean doesn't.

Once you've written one of these, you start recognising the shape everywhere:.

None of those require a different model. They're the same 33 coordinates with different geometry sitting on top, and the geometry is a few dozen lines each.

Here's why I keep insisting on the distinction between coordinates and meaning.

When my rep counter miscounts, I don't retrain anything. I don't collect a dataset, I don't label examples, I don't spin up a training job. I look at two things: my thresholds, and my state machine. One of them is wrong.

That's a normal bug in normal code, and you already know how to find it. You can log the angle. You can set a breakpoint on the transition. You can write a unit test that feeds a synthetic sequence of angles through update and asserts the count — no camera, no model, no fixtures:.

According to recent reports, the hard part of this problem — turning pixels into joint positions — was solved by a research team and shipped to you as a file you can download. The part that's left is the part you're already good at.

In a recent development, you are not blocked on machine learning knowledge. You were blocked on nobody telling you this was available.

I set delegate: 'GPU' above without comment, and it deserves one. MediaPipe Tasks lets you choose between a CPU path and a GPU path, and availability of the GPU path varies by browser, platform and graphics driver.

The practical consequence is that you have to test the CPU path, because for some meaningful share of your owners it isn't a fallback — it's the only path they will ever take. If you develop on a machine where the GPU delegate works and never exercise the CPU one, you have shipped something you've never run.

That, and the question of how often you should run the model at all, is a bigger subject than this article. It's the next one.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kagi is best known as a paid alternative to Google Search, but the company is now introducing its own email service that offers an alternative to Gmail.

It has been revealed that kagi Mail has been in the works for a long time, the firm says in a post today, but it’s only just now launching in public beta. Owners get an “@kagimail.com” address or can use their own domain, with both email and a calendar included.

There’s a 60-day trial for Kagi Mail, with the service costing $99.99/year (or included in Kagi’s $25/month Ultimate initiative). The reason you’d pay that, Kagi explains, is because this is a product designed to “do its job and then get out of your way,” with no ads or “surveillance” as a part of the package.

Does the world need another email service? We asked ourselves that question more than once. There are great ones out there, and we’re fans of what Fastmail and Tuta are doing. We still built our own, for the same reason we build everything at Kagi: technology should do its job and then get out of your way.

For email, that job is to be fast, private, and secure. On top of that, it should help you stay on track with what’s crucial: bring forward what you need to act on, respond to, or acknowledge, and quietly handle the rest.

There’s a mobile app coming for Kagi Mail in early 2027, with a contact book and Kagi Assistant integration also slated for early next year. There is some natural language AI for organization, blocking of tracking pixels and remote images by default, and support for email clients like Apple Mail, and Kagi indicates everything can be exported to move to another provider should you choose.

Are you going to give it a try?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The United States Department of Justice announced today that more than 800 defendants have been charged and over $8 billion in intended victim losses have been recovered in what it describes as the "largest ever" crackdown on scammers and fraudsters in its history. The charges have led to over 400 cases, filed across 85 federal districts, with outcomes including extraditions, guilty pleas, and prison sentences for those involved.

According to recent reports, "We are not just going after individual scammers," Fox News reports U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche as saying. "We are dismantling the criminal networks that have been stealing from the American people for far too long.".

The push follows President Donald Trump's executive order from March, which required a government-wide crackdown on the kinds of fraud and predatory schemes that people fall victim to each and every day across the country.

It has been revealed that FBI Director Kash Patel also gave details of Operation Blackout, an interagency project that targets international fraudsters running centralized facilities. Patel stated that FBI agents, alongside their international counterparts, have dismantled 29 centralized compounds across Asia, Africa, and the Middle East. The department claims those agents have seized almost $17 billion in funds, that more than 14,000 involved devices have been confiscated, and that 50 "scam actors" have been brought up on U.S. federal charges. The FBI also says its support allowed its foreign partners to arrest or detain more than 320 criminals in foreign jurisdictions.

In a recent development, perhaps most importantly, these compounds often use human trafficking victims to run online scams. Patel claims that more than 2,200 trafficked workers have been freed as a result of the initiative.

Global scams and hacking are an ongoing problem for the United States and its citizens, not to mention its businesses, big and small. Just last month, more than $5 million in gift cards were stolen from Staples before being used at retailers like Target and Lowes. A Chinese crime ring was behind that attack, which involved more than 15,000 cards.

Earlier this year, a Chinese phishing service was dismantled after it used AI tools to build scam websites linked to almost $2 billion in losses. An October report even detailed a computer, hidden behind a Japanese hotel room fridge, that was responsible for more than 480,000 phishing emails.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

The problem is only likely to get worse as the capabilities and availability of AI tools continue to expand. U.S. banks have scrambled to restrict AI agent activity over concerns about what they could do to customer accounts. Some banks raised the alarm after detecting agents accessing customer accounts and even attempting to process transactions. Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, JPMorgan, and Wells Fargo are among those that have blocked the agents while updating their terms of service accordingly.

That growing threat only emphasizes the fact that the department has much work left to do. The $17 billion seized by the FBI is only a portion of the estimated $68 billion Americans lost to scams in 2025, according to Gallup data, so the ongoing game of cat and mouse between the government and criminal enterprises the world over will only continue.

Google Maps has a pretty consistent style, but a newly introduced option appears to be in the works with a darker “high-visibility” setting.

Sources indicate that the last major change to Google Maps styling came in 2023 (yes, time flies) when the platform rolled out a latest color palette to all users. This was divisive among users, but ultimately worked out.

Now, Google appears to be working on another new shake-up.

The folks over at Android Authority spotted a new “high-visibility” toggle in the latest Google Maps update for Android, with the new style having darker colors for the map in both light and dark modes, as well as a purple line for your route compared to the blue we’re used to seeing.

The change was also spotted on Android Auto, with much darker colors (including a near-black dark mode) in both color settings for your car’s display. This is likely tied to this new “High-visibility” setting, but it’s hard to say for certain – teardowns and enabling new features early can only tell us so much.

Sources indicate that this appears to all be controlled by a latest “Map style” setting in Google Maps, with “Standard” and “High-visibility” settings available. Functionally, everything remains the same, it’s just a new set of colors.

So, where the previous color changes were forced on all owners, this one is at least optional, and the “High-visibility” naming seems like it’s targeted at those with difficulties in sight more so than just a general change for all users.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The MDR-3R are Sony’s revival of the wired over-ear headphones that many used with a classic Walkman player.
  • Patch 11/24: After we first published our hands-on with MDR-3R last week, Sony’s USB-C headphones sold out pretty quickly again.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sony’s iconic Walkman headphones are back in the USB-C MDR-3R and, after promptly selling out on launch day, they’ve now been restocked. And, after using them, I can see why they sold out so quickly.

The MDR-3R are Sony’s revival of the wired over-ear headphones that many used with a classic Walkman player. The retro style still looks great in 2026, but using an original pair is a bit of a headache in today’s age of headphone jack-less smartphones. So it was nice to see Sony give this a revival with USB-C.

And, yeah, they live up to the hype.

Patch 11/24: After we first published our hands-on with MDR-3R last week, Sony’s USB-C headphones sold out pretty quickly again. As of today, though, they’re back in stock and still shipping in early December – don’t miss out!

While the style won’t be for everyone, I think these work brilliantly. The sound quality is excellent and having a pair of headphones that doesn’t fully enclose my ears is pretty refreshing. There’s no noise cancellation, but with open-ear earbuds becoming more popular, I actually really like these as a similar solution (though high volumes will definitely be heard by those around you). I’m not fully cut off from the world around me, but I’m also able to get good sound quality. Lows are the weakness here, with unimpressive bass drops, but the sound quality is crisp and clear and pretty neutral, and the open-ish style makes it feel like the room around me is filled with music.

Recent findings suggest that the physical hardware is great. While a plastic and metal build is objectively not as comfy as a premium pair of ANC headphones, the extremely light weight helps MDR-3R become an afterthought. You simply forget you’re wearing them after a few minutes.

The earpads are swappable, with orange and blue options included in the box.

As for the USB-C cable, it’s fully plug-and-play. No app needed and it worked across every device I tested (including Pixel, which doesn’t work with all USB-C audio output). I do wish the cable was perhaps a few inches longer, but it’s long enough to wear the headphones with my phone in my front pocket. There’s a remote along the cable for play/pause and volume adjustments, though I think it’s a little too high on the cable.

According to recent reports, for $59.99, these are a fun pair of USB-C headphones to have on hand. They sound good, work great, and don’t cost an arm and a leg. I can see why they sold out so quickly on launch day – in just 10 hours, Sony told me.

According to recent reports, sony MDR-3R are back in stock now and shipping in early December. If you want a pair, I say don’t wait. They’re well worth at least trying if you can get them for retail price – please don’t give in to the scalpers selling these at double, they’re not worth that.

#195241. Building the Hugging Face MCP Server

Building the Hugging Face MCP Server

📅 10 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1415 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, TL;DR: The Hugging Face Official MCP Server offers unique customization options for AI Assistants accessing the Hub, along with access to thousands of AI applications through one simple URL.
  • We've learned many things about building a useful MCP server in the last month - we'll describe our journey here.
  • The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is fulfilling its promise of being the standard to connect AI Assistants to the outside world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, TL;DR: The Hugging Face Official MCP Server offers unique customization options for AI Assistants accessing the Hub, along with access to thousands of AI applications through one simple URL. We used MCPs "Streamable HTTP" transport for deployment, and examine in detail the trade-offs that Server Developers have.

We've learned many things about building a useful MCP server in the last month - we'll describe our journey here.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is fulfilling its promise of being the standard to connect AI Assistants to the outside world.

At Hugging Face, providing access to the Hub via MCP is an obvious choice, and this article shares our experience developing the hf.co/mcp MCP Server.

The community uses the Hub for research, development, content creation and more. We wanted to let people customize the server for their own needs, as well as easily access thousands of AI applications available on Spaces. This meant making the MCP Server dynamic by adjusting users' tools on the fly.

We also wanted to make access simple by avoiding complicated downloads and configuration, so making it remotely accessible via a simple URL was a must.

It has been revealed that when building a remote MCP Server, the first decision is deciding how clients will connect to it. MCP offers several transport options, with different trade-offs. TL;DR: our open source code supports all variants, but for production we chose to go with the most modern one. This section goes through the different options in detail.

Industry observers note that since its launch in November 2024, MCP has undergone rapid evolution with 3 protocol revisions in 9 months. This has seen the replacement of the SSE Transport with Streamable HTTP, as well as the introduction and rework of authorization.

These rapid changes mean support for different MCP Features and revisions in Client applications varies, providing extra challenges for our design choices.

Here is a brief summary of the Transport Options offered by the Model Context Protocol and associated SDKs:.

Both STDIO and HTTP with SSE are fully bi-directional by default - meaning that Client and Server maintain an open connection and can send messages to each other at any time.

SSE refers to "Server Sent Events" - a way for HTTP Servers to maintain an open connection and send events in response to a request.

MCP Server Developers face a lot of choices when setting up the Streamable HTTP transport.

There are 3 main communication patterns to choose from:.

When using Request Scoped Streams with the official SDKs, use the sendNotification() and sendRequest() methods provided in the RequestHandlerExtra parameter (TypeScript) or set the related_request_id (Python) to send messages to the correct stream.

An additional factor to consider is whether or not the MCP Server itself needs to maintain state for each connection. This is decided by the Server when the Client sends its Initialize request:.

The table below summarizes the MCP Features and their supported communication pattern:.

With Request Scoped streams, Sampling and Elicitation requests need a Stateful connection so that the mcp-session-id can be used for response association.

The Hugging Face MCP Server is Open Source - and supports STDIO, SSE and Streamable HTTP deployment in both Direct Response and Server Push mode. You can configure keep-alive and last activity timeouts when using Server Push Streams. There's also a built-in observability dashboard that you can use to understand how different Clients manage connections, and handle Tool List change notifications.

The following picture demonstrates our MCP Server connection dashboard running in "Server Push" Streamable HTTP mode:.

For production, we decided to launch our MCP Server with Streamable HTTP in a Stateless, Direct Response configuration for the following reasons:.

According to recent reports, stateless For anonymous people we supply a standard set of Tools for using the Hub along with an Image Generator. For authenticated users our state comprises their selected tools and chosen Gradio applications. We also make sure that users ZeroGPU quota is correctly applied for their account. This is managed using the supplied HF_TOKEN or OAuth credentials that we look up on request. None of our existing tools require us to maintain any other state between requests.

Sources indicate that you can use OAuth login by adding ?login to the MCP Server url - e.g. https://huggingface.co/mcp?login. We may make this the default once the claude.ai remote integration supports the latest OAuth spec.

Direct Response provides the lowest deployment resource overhead - and we don't right now have any Tools that require Sampling or Elicitation during execution.

Sources indicate that future Support At launch, the "HTTP with SSE" transport was still the remote default in a lot of MCP Clients. However, we didn't want to invest heavily in managing it due to its imminent deprecation. Fortunately, popular clients had already started making the switch (VSCode and Cursor), and within a week of launch claude.ai also added support. If you need to connect with SSE, feel free to deploy a copy of our Server on a FreeCPU Hugging Face Space.

In the future, we would like to support real-time Tool List Changed notifications when users upgrade their settings on the Hub. However, this raises a couple of practical issues:.

First, customers tend to configure their favourite MCP Servers in their Client and leave them enabled. This means that the Client remains connected whilst the application is open. Sending notifications would mean maintaining as many open connections as there were currently active Clients - regardless of active usage - on the chance the user updates their tool configuration.

Second, most MCP Servers and Clients disconnect after a period of inactivity, resuming when necessary. This inevitably means that immediate push notifications would be missed - as the notification channel will have been closed. In practice, it is far simpler for the Client to refresh the connection and Tool List as needed.

Unless you have reasonable control over the Client/Server pair, using Server Push Streams adds a lot of complexity to a public deployment, when lower-resource solutions for refreshing the Tool List exist.

Just before launch, @julien-c submitted a PR to include friendly instructions for customers visiting hf.co/mcp. This hugely improves the User Experience - the default response is otherwise an unfriendly bit of JSON.

Initially, we found this generated an enormous amount of traffic. After a bit of investigation we found that when returning a web page rather than an HTTP 405 error, VSCode would poll the endpoint multiple times per second!

Industry observers note that the fix suggested by @coyotte508 was to properly detect browsers and only return the page in that circumstance. Thanks also to the VSCode team who rapidly fixed it.

Although not specifically stated - returning a page in this manner does seem acceptable within the MCP Specification.

The MCP Protocol sends several requests during initialization. A typical connection sequence is: Initialize, Notifications/Initialize, tools/list and then prompts/list.

Given that MCP Clients will connect and reconnect whilst open, and the fact that owners make periodic calls, we find there is a ratio of around 100 MCP Control messages for each Tool Call.

Some clients also send requests that don't make sense for our Stateless, Direct Response configuration - for example Pings, Cancellations or attempts to list Resources (which isn't a capability we currently advertise).

According to recent reports, the first week of July 2025 saw an astonishing 164 different Clients accessing our Server. Interestingly, one of the most popular tools is mcp-remote. Approximately half of all Clients use it as a bridge to connect to our remote server.

MCP is rapidly evolving, and we're excited about what has already been achieved across Chat Applications, IDEs, Agents and MCP Servers over the last few months.

We can already see how powerful integrating the Hugging Face Hub has been and support for Gradio Spaces now makes it possible for LLMs to be easily extended with the latest Machine Learning applications.

Here are some great examples of things people have been doing with our MCP Server so far:.

We hope that this post has provided insights to the decisions that need to be made building Remote MCP Servers, and encourage you to try some of the examples in your favourite MCP Client.

Take a look at our Open Source MCP Server, and try some of the different transport options with your Client, or open an Concern or Pull Request to make improvements or suggest latest functionality.

Let us know your thoughts, feedback and questions on this discussion thread.

The original Gemini integration in Google Messages dates back to 2024 with a dedicated FAB (floating action button) above Start chat. It lets you have a straightforward conversation with Gemini.

This updated experience makes use of the “Channels” feature introduced last week that allows you to Text or Email with Gemini to accomplish tasks.

According to recent reports, with the latest Google Messages beta (version 20261120_01_RC00), we’re seeing the Gemini FAB (or top-right corner icon with the homepage redesign) open gemini.google.com/channels on a fresh install. Sources indicate that after using it for the past few days, the proactive nature of Gemini tasks in Google Messages has really stood out. Every morning, Gemini messages me about what’s on my schedule or what should be on my radar. Examples include:.

While this instance of Gemini is ostensibly for tasks, I’ve been able to ask general knowledge questions, like about the weather, similar to the old experience. Additionally, you can upload attachments like images and files.

This new Google Messages integration is presently available in the US and requires that you have tasks enabled in the Gemini app.

Sources indicate that when using the out-of-the-box Gemini Enterprise web application, identity and access management happen behind the scenes. Employees sign in through Google Identity or Workforce Identity Federation (such as Microsoft Entra ID or Okta), search results automatically respect per-user access controls (ACLs), and third-party login prompts for Federated Connectors or custom agents appear automatically in the chat UI.

According to recent reports, in practice, however, many enterprises build their own Customer UI to embed Gemini Enterprise into an internal portal, intranet, or line-of-business application. To do this, Customer BE calls the Gemini Enterprise StreamAssist API.

The moment an application builds a custom UI and calls the StreamAssist API directly, the three authentication flows that the built-in web app handled automatically become the responsibility of Customer UI and Customer BE:.
