InferNode gives Bell Labs' Inferno OS a 64-bit second wind

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1155 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Plan 9's successor finds a latest role containing AI agents, though its developer notes those features are optional.
  • InferNode brings a modernized, 64-bit edition of Inferno, the distributed operating system that followed Proposal 9 from Bell Labs.
  • Recent findings suggest that for us, the strapline of the InferNode project distracts from the interesting part.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Plan 9's successor finds a latest role containing AI agents, though its developer notes those features are optional.

InferNode brings a modernized, 64-bit edition of Inferno, the distributed operating system that followed Proposal 9 from Bell Labs.

Recent findings suggest that for us, the strapline of the InferNode project distracts from the interesting part. It describes the project as a "Secure Runtime for AI Agents," but we think it's something far more interesting than another LLM tool.

Fair warning: this vulture has no interest whatsoever in AI agents, and we are not even going to look at this planned use of InferNode. We're interested in the OS, and here, its GitHub repository spells out the part that caught our attention: "a 64-bit Inferno® OS.".

That grabbed us because Inferno is a very interesting OS, although it doesn't get much attention – for example, the official Inferno GitHub repository shows little activity in the last few years.

Inferno is the successor to Plan 9, which we've written and talked about before, including recent releases of its community continuation, 9front.

Industry observers note that initiative 9 is what the team who invented Unix did next. Plan 9 is a very minimalist, natively clustered Unix: machines can freely mount one another's filesystems, display windows on one another, and start processes on one another. Plan 9 turns a network of machines running this Unix-like OS into a single machine. So, for instance, if you were working on a laptop with limited storage and compute power, you could compile a large complex project on a faster machine elsewhere on the network, using project files located on a third machine, while watching the process in your terminal on your screen, with no messing about with SSH sessions.

Strategy 9 and 9front programs are compiled into architecture-specific native binaries. Different processor families can still work together across the network, but the same executable won't run unchanged on both an x86-64 laptop and an Arm64 server.

Sources indicate that inferno takes a different approach. It's contemporaneous with the far less ambitious Java. On Inferno, languages compile code for a VM called Dis, which is part of the kernel. This means that Inferno binaries execute directly on anything that the Inferno kernel runs on. The OS kernel is built to run bare-metal, or as a process on various other OSes, without needing a separate hardware virtual machine or hypervisor.

It has been revealed that A single binary can run on all supported CPU architectures. Inferno applications are normally written in the Limbo programming language, whose documentation was written by Unix co-creator Dennis Ritchie. Limbo is one of the languages that influenced Go, but Inferno lets compilers for other languages target Dis as well. The binaries run anywhere. Inferno on Arm, or x86, or RISC-V, or running in a Windows or Linux or macOS process, your program just runs.

Recent findings suggest that we've been trying to contact Vita Nuova, the tech giant that maintains Inferno, for some years without success. Development appears to have slowed considerably. Moving the runtime to 64-bit also raises compatibility questions: some forks change Dis's word size and cannot run existing 32-bit bytecode unchanged.

According to recent reports, we're aware of several efforts to build 64-bit versions of Inferno. Caerwyn Jones's Inferno64 is one of the more visible, and the GitHub repository (and indeed his X account) show considerable activity. However, Inferno64's Dis is not compatible with 32-bit Dis code. Another fork is Dinsmoor's Inferno64, which also demonstrates recent activity, albeit with the assistance of the Claude LLM. Others include the long-quiescent Purgatorio and 9ferno, both inactive for years, plus Scott Guyon's more active fork. Dropping the compatibility goal altogether, Node9 replaces Limbo with Lua and Dis with LuaJIT.

It has been revealed that there are more forks and variants than we've gone into here. Given that there have been quite a few efforts, and most haven't delivered final ready-to-use products yet, we were surprised when InferNode was suddenly unveiled on the Inferno-OS mailing list last week.

Developer Peter Finn stated: "An experimental runtime for containing generative AI agents was the original motivation, but most of the work since has been on the OS itself, and the AI parts are ordinary file servers. For example, llmsrv at /mnt/llm and speech9p are started from the login profile, and if you delete those lines they're simply not there. There's also non-generative AI additions on object detection served as files at /mnt/vision, on the CPU or a GPU host, and voice calls between devices done by mounting each other's audio files over 9P. There's a GUI layer intended to facilitate hands-free AI agent use, but it too is optional.".

He also said that InferNode's development was largely independent of the existing efforts, partly because the primary target was Arm64, not x86-64. Its 64-bit Dis runtime is incompatible with the 32-bit original: "The opcodes, file format and magic number are unchanged, but the word size isn't, so frame sizes, offsets and pointer maps all differ. Limbo source recompiles without edits. A 32-bit .dis is at the moment rejected at load time.".

It has been revealed that inferNode doesn't implement 9front's DP9IK authentication protocol, so it cannot connect to servers requiring that authentication. Dr Finn told us: "DP9IK is not quantum-safe. That's the reason. InferNode's current crypto policy is strict CNSA.".

InferNode also includes some slightly unexpected components, related to its intended use for testing LLM agents – such as a wallet for the Ethereum cryptocurrency, which Finn noted was "mainly to support agent payments.".

In a recent development, the first release of Inferno was in 1996, the year after Java and the JVM were launched. Inferno is a much more ambitious project, but its core function – the ability to run identical binaries on multiple platforms, without recompilation – was close enough that they ended up competing in the market, and Java won. It was a pleasant surprise to see a modernized version of Inferno arrive this year, 30 years on.

Sources indicate that finn told us: "About a year ago I saw the potential for a 'break-out' moment for this tech as a runtime for containing AI agents. The flood of cybersecurity risks we would face on account of adversarial AI agents required new systems with small footprints and minimal attack surfaces. Inferno was a perfect candidate and it was an opportunity to show the world how visionary Plan 9's ideas were and how well they mapped on to pressing contemporary security issues.".

"If InferNode succeeds, it is an opportunity for Blueprint 9's ideas to migrate out of hobby-land and really make an impact – as they deservedly should.".

He has a point. On a related note, this vulture discussed the possibility of rebuilding the world's IT systems from scratch on last week's Kettle podcast. Perhaps the hour for tools like this really has come round at last. ®.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In this blog post, we talk about all the upgrades in-depth, and how they become part of the transformers toolkit so other models (current and future) can benefit from them.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OpenAI recently released their GPT-OSS series of models. The models feature some novel techniques like MXFP4 quantization, efficient kernels, a brand fresh chat format, and more. To enable the release of gpt-oss through transformers, we have upgraded the library considerably. The updates make it very efficient to load, run, and fine-tune the models.

In this blog post, we talk about all the upgrades in-depth, and how they become part of the transformers toolkit so other models (current and future) can benefit from them. Providing clean implementations of newly introduced methods in transformers also allows the community to quickly understand and adopt them. Frameworks such as MLX, llama.cpp or vLLM can use the transformers code as a reference to build their own implementations.

For this release, we worked on:.

Best part: Most of these features should work across all major models within transformers!

Recent findings suggest that A kernel is a specialized, compact program that runs on accelerators to execute tasks like matrix multiplications, activations, or normalizations. In eager PyTorch, operations trigger individual kernels sequentially, which is straightforward but can incur extra memory transfers and launch overheads. PyTorch 2.0's torch.compile with backends like TorchInductor addresses this by automatically fusing and optimizing kernels, delivering 2–10× performance gains.

In a recent development, in addition, the community has created custom kernels for frequent combinations of operations, not just individual PyTorch ops like matmul. For example, Flash Attention was created to optimize the critical attention block that defines the transformers architecture, and is present in many models including most LLMs. By carefully combining all the attention operations inside a single kernel, memory transfers are minimized, memory use is reduced, and speedups can be achieved.

In a recent development, the problem is that all these various kernels are available in separate libraries, which creates a dependency bloat if they were to be added to the transformers library. Furthermore, these kernels are not just Python code, they consist of low-level cuda code, glued together with C++ and exposed through a Python layer. This means they have to be compiled in the target system, which in turn requires whatever build system is required by each kernel library.

In a recent development, the kernels package solves this problem by downloading pre-built binaries of supported kernels from the Hub. You just indicate the kernel you want to use, and kernels will look for a version compatible with your system and download it on first use.

GPT-OSS, a Mixture of Experts (MoE) model, is a major user of Kernels from the Hub. It leverages several custom kernels:.

Let's take a look at the first two ones.

Industry observers note that behind the scenes, the decorators (1 and 2) simply point to community-contributed kernels. For example, RMSNorm comes from liger_kernels, while the MegaBlocksMoeMLP kernel comes from megablocks. Depending on your device (CUDA or ROCm) and whether you’re training or running inference, the right kernel is pulled in automatically.

This design is both specific and general: the RMSNorm liger kernels are already being reused across multiple models, and the MoE kernel could be applied to future MoEs as well.

Recent findings suggest that because kernels pulls code from the Hub, you have to opt-in to this feature by passing use_kernels=True in your model instantiation, as shown below. We enable INFO logging in the example so you can easily verify that downloadable kernels are in use.

According to recent reports, these kernels are not compatible with mxfp4, so inference will happen in bfloat16 if you use them. Please, benchmark your system for the best combination in memory and throughput that suits your project!

OpenAI gpt-oss models use attention sinks, which improves quality and facilitates the use of longer contexts. The vLLM team added this feature to the latest version of Flash Attention (Flash Attention 3), and the resulting custom kernel is available on the Hub. Presently, this kernel is compatible with the Hopper architecture. If you have one, this is the way to enable it:.

Recent findings suggest that large language models are memory-hungry. Quantization reduces memory footprint by storing weights (and sometimes activations) in lower-precision formats. For reference, FP32 uses 32 bits per number and BF16 uses 16. By reducing bit width, we trade some precision for smaller models and faster memory movement.

If you want a visual primer on quantization trade-offs, Maarten Grootendorst’s article is excellent: A Visual Guide to Quantization.

MXFP4 is a 4-bit floating format with E2M1 layout: 1 sign bit, 2 exponent bits, and 1 mantissa bit, as shown in Figure 2. On its own, E2M1 is very coarse. MXFP4 compensates with blockwise scaling:.

Industry observers note that this blockwise scheme lets MXFP4 keep range while using very few bits. In practice, GPT-OSS 20B fits in roughly 16 GB of VRAM and GPT-OSS 120B fits in roughly 80 GB when MXFP4 is active, which is the difference between “cannot load” and “can run on a single GPU.” The catch is that matrix multiplies now have to respect block scales. Doing this efficiently at scale requires dedicated kernels.

transformers now includes native support for MXFP4, leveraging optimized triton (MXFP4) kernels for enhanced performance. This builds on the community-driven kernel distribution discussed earlier, utilizing pre-compiled kernels from the Hub to simplify deployment.

To check if a model supports MXFP4, inspect its configuration:.

If 'quant_method': 'mxfp4' is present, the model will automatically use the MXFP4 pathway with Triton kernels when supported.

Thanks to this pull request, you can fine-tune gpt-oss models and save them directly to the Hub in MXFP4 format, streamlining deployment with optimized performance.

If these constraints are not met, transformers falls back to a higher-precision path (bfloat16 is used by default), which requires about 4× the memory of MXFP4.

The snippet loads GPT-OSS twice on CUDA: once with Mxfp4Config(dequantize=True) (memory intensive) and once in the default quantized path (memory efficient). Figure 3 shows the amount of used VRAM after each load so you can visualize the savings.

In a recent development, efficient MXFP4 requires kernels that understand 32-element blocks and their scales during GEMMs and fused ops. This is where Kernels from the Hub comes in again. transformers automatically pulls in the MXFP4-aware Triton kernels from the community repository when you load a model that needs them. The repository will appear in your local cache and will be used during the forward pass. For the MXFP4 kernels one does not need to use the use_kernels=True parameter like before, it is set to default in transformers.

Quick sanity check with the Hugging Face cache CLI, after running gpt-oss-20b on a GPU compatible with the triton MXFP4 kernels:.

This indicates the MXFP4 kernels were fetched and are available for execution.

Sources indicate that let's run some benchmarks and see how well the MXFP4 kernels perform. In Figure 4, we see that the MXFP4 kernels are even better than the custom MoE and RMSNorm kernels for larger batches.

You can explore and play with the benchmarking script here.

Tensor Parallelism (TP) splits tensors inside a layer across multiple GPUs (as shown in Figure 5). Each GPU multiplies its shard in parallel, and then partial results are collected using all-gather or all-reduce operations. This reduces per-GPU memory and keeps all GPUs working on the same layer, which improves throughput as sequence length or batch size grow. TP is communication-intensive and generally works best on a single machine with fast intra-node links.

transformers implements TP directly in from_pretrained. You can start with the predefined plan:.

If you don’t have the infrastructure to run the above, you can just spawn a process on our GPUs using Hugging Face Jobs!

hf jobs is available for all Hugging Face PRO & Enterprise users.

Sources indicate that under the hood, tp_plan="auto" selects a predefined sharding recipe for each layer and wires the necessary collectives. You can inspect the active plan with print(model._tp_plan) if you want to verify what is being sharded.

Recent findings suggest that use TP when the model is too large for one GPU and you want parallel compute, not only memory placement. TP tends to scale throughput with more GPUs, especially for long sequences or larger batches.

If you are curious about how TP differs from device_map="auto" (memory placement), this short Stack Overflow answer explains the distinction and when to use each.

To learn more about TP, here are two must-read resources:.

Expert Parallelism (EP) shards experts inside MoE layers across GPUs. Each token is routed to one or a few experts, so only those experts run their feed-forward pass. Since experts are independent MLPs, we can place different experts on different ranks and exchange only the hidden states for the routed tokens. This keeps the matrix multiplies intact on each rank and replaces tensor slicing with routing and collectives.

In a recent development, run with multiple processes using torchrun. EP is enabled via the distributed configuration and works with GPT-OSS MoE layers out of the box in transformers.

Here is how you would run using hf jobs.

Recent findings suggest that when you enable Expert Parallelism, Tensor Parallelism is also activated. This means you enjoy the best of both worlds!

Many recent LLMs use sliding window attention, or a combination of sliding and global attention layers, as a means to save memory and reduce those expensive quadratic matmuls that grow with sequence length. However, the dynamic KV cache implementation in transformers used to continue to allocate space according to sequence length, without looking at the individual attention layers. You could always optimize memory using compilation (meaning, fixed shapes), but that's a separate scenario altogether.

In a recent development, transformers now has a DynamicSlidingWindowLayer and a config‑aware DynamicCache. If the model config declares sliding‑window or hybrid attention (both sliding and global attention layers are used), the cache stops growing past the window for the sliding layers. If you don’t pass the config, behavior stays as before (full, ever‑growing KV as sequence length grows).

For models that only use sliding window layers, such as Mistral 7B, cache memory stops growing when the sequence reaches the window size (4096, in this case). This makes sense, because the sliding layers can't look past the previous 4K tokens anyway.

Recent findings suggest that openAI gpt-oss alternates between sliding and global attention layers, which results in total KV cache memory being halved, as we'll see, as sequence length increases. This provides us with:.

Recent findings suggest that the optimized cache is set by default, that means you don't have to make any changes to your existing code. If you want to create the DynamicCache explicitly here is how you would do it:.

Figure 6 showcases how much of a difference it makes for us to use the Dynamic KV Cache with sliding window attention.

A typical autoregressive generation process looks like Figure 7. You input the prefill tokens, and the model predicts each new token one after the other until it predicts the EOS (End of Sequence) token.

According to recent reports, let’s see what the generation process looks like when we pass a batch of inputs. In Figure 8 you notice that some generations finish off earlier than the others. This mismatch of length underutilizes the GPUs.

Industry observers note that this type of batching sequences is called static batching. While this is simple and easy to understand, it inherently comes with inefficiencies. Only after each sentence is completely generated can we move on to the next batch.

According to recent reports, to bypass this matter, we use dynamic batching (also known as continuous batching). Instead of waiting for all the generation to finish, we schedule incoming requests to the completed generations. That way, as soon as a generation in a batch is complete, we prefill the batch with the next request. The process looks like Figure 9.

Transformers supports continuous batching with the generate_batch API. This is not meant for production-grade model serving –frameworks like vLLM and SGLang are great at that–, but can be very helpful for evaluation and experimentation. Here is an example script that runs CB end to end on Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507.

Sources indicate that we have also performed a benchmark between Continuous Batching and Static Batching with 100 samples. In Figure 9, we note that CB is quite faster than SB.

You can play around with the benchmark here: SB, CB.

When you load a large model into your GPU, PyTorch needs to reserve GPU memory for each layer’s weights. Each of these requests (per layer) takes time, and for multi-billion-parameter models it can mean thousands of tiny memory allocations, adding up to a long wait before the model is ready. Instead of asking the GPU for new memory every single time, it can hold on to a significant chunk once and then hand out slices from it quickly.

PyTorch allocators can do exactly this. The catch is that the allocator only gets fast after you’ve given it some memory to work with. If you don’t “stock the pantry” first, you still end up doing many slow trips to the market. This PR (🎉 #36380) taught transformers to pre-stock the pantry before it starts copying model weights.

Recent findings suggest that you have to make no changes to your existing code, as this is default behaviour in transformers. If you use device_map="auto" or provide your own device map, your model will now load faster automatically. If you’re running with Tensor Parallel (tp_plan="auto") and torchrun you also benefit from companion changes that make multi-GPU loading smarter.

Recent findings suggest that transformers moves swiftly and it is community-first. The library evolves at the pace of the field because contributors shape it in the open. Pieces added for new models become part of the toolkit and are reused in future integrations.

Industry observers note that this velocity enables day-zero integrations like the GPT-OSS series. As the stack becomes increasingly PyTorch-first, it trims bloat and doubles down on the PyTorch paths that matter in practice. The result is a cleaner core that unlocks newly introduced capabilities through community kernels, quantization, and parallelism plans, while also standardizing model definitions so that architectures supported in transformers are a reference and extend across the wider ecosystem.

In a recent development, this post is a one-time snapshot of a process we repeatedly iterate on towards the same direction: serve the needs of the community. To be up to date with the latest additions to transformers, check the docs and release notes. And please, keep sharing your feedback and releasing your models in transformers for the community to enjoy 🤗.

If you want to go further into particular topics, here is a list of links that one should visit:.

In my own experiments, I applied quantization to a mmalam786/distilbert-sst2-int8-onnx-demo and saw ~20-30% latency reduction with negligible accuracy drop. Do you have insights on how MXFP4 handles activation quantization vs weight quantization in edge scenarios? Happy to share my demo if useful: https://www.linkedin.com/posts/dr-mm-alam-93991120b_demofirst-aichips-edgeai-activity-7381674484098883584-0Rwn/?utm_source=share&utm_medium=member_desktop&rcm=ACoAADVZuP0BheDJgKL8dWk-bNo7Yd4zhsOnNL4.

PyTorch now natively supports Flash Attention. I created a PR to add Flash Attention support for GPT-OSS:.

https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/42345.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NOTICE: Sneakernet is a work in progress. The documentation makes some promises that are not reflected in the current state of affairs. Links to to-be-written parts of the documentation are indicated in red.

Sneakernet is a system for securely1 sending digital messages to other people without using the Internet. Instead, messages are automatically passed on to other Sneakernet users on your local network – at your hackerspace, an event or conference, your local cafe, etc — and then physically carried to their destination on your “sneakers”, where they will be automatically delivered to any recipients on the same network (or handed over to be carried further on by someone else).

Sneakernet encourages slow, thoughtful participation in community and face-to-face meetings with the people who will carry your messages onwards to their destination, and entrust their own messages to you.

⇒ Head to Getting started to set up Sneakernet on your device.

Recent findings suggest that many applications can be built on top of sneakernet’s general-purpose messaging system, provided that they are tolerant of high latency and out-of-order messages. Some examples include:.

Building your own sneakernet applications is easy, too, in any programming language – see Building applications for more details.

All messages are authenticated and all private messages are also encrypted. People who carry your messages along cannot tamper with them and cannot read your private messages. See Security for more details.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that easy-to-use, popular, not collecting data for us, or serving our ads?
  • Arm is swinging the hammer at an enthusiast’s site hosting a bloat-free version of its instruction reference documentation, demanding it be taken offline after several years of availability.
  • The demand from Arm lawyers to Jon Palmisciano concern Jon’s Arm Reference, a site that provides the same arm Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) info available on Arm’s site, but with what Palmisciano describes as “without a million popups and all of the bloat” that Arm provides on its own.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that easy-to-use, popular, not collecting data for us, or serving our ads? Down with you!

Arm is swinging the hammer at an enthusiast’s site hosting a bloat-free version of its instruction reference documentation, demanding it be taken offline after several years of availability.

The demand from Arm lawyers to Jon Palmisciano concern Jon’s Arm Reference, a site that provides the same arm Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) info available on Arm’s site, but with what Palmisciano describes as “without a million popups and all of the bloat” that Arm provides on its own.

According to Palmisciano, his copy of the Arm ISA was culled from machine-readable XML files and stripped of the bloat. He built his version in 2022 with latest CSS on top of it, and the addition of a quick search feature that, according to his comments on Hacker News, isn’t available in the official version.

Recent findings suggest that “The aim has always been to make it the most comfortable and bullshit-free browsing experience for people who need these docs daily,” Palmisciano wrote in HN. Based on the responses the site seems to have plenty of fans.

Arm doesn’t care if Palmisciano’s project is well intentioned or for the benefit of the many software developers that write code for its chipsets, either: They want it offline by December 4 – 10 days from the publication of this story – or else.

As for what is going to happen, it seems like Jon’s Arm Reference will likely cease to exist in a little over a week – at least in its current form.

In a recent development, “Ideally I'd love to just get permission from Arm to keep the site up, but I'm pretty pessimistic about that,” Palmisciano told us. That stated, Palmisciano has “already seen a few archives and mirrors already.” The HN thread discussing the takedown order includes links to several versions, and Palmisciano has another trick up his sleeve that he’s considering playing: Open-sourcing the software he used to build his ISA page.

According to recent reports, “I'd also consider open-sourcing my tooling so that people can (for their own private use) turn the original XML downloads from Arm into an identical site they can host locally,” Palmisciano told us. He stated that he'll likely tweet about opening the tooling if he does do so. He's also considered directing the URL for Jon's Arm reference to point to the open-source tool, but Arm wants the subdomain it's hosted on removed from his site as well, so that may not happen.

Arm has been in touch to defend itself as well, saying that Arm appreciates the efforts of people like Palmisciano, but that it still has to protect its brand, and documentation.

In other words, if you’re an Arm dev worried about losing a valuable resource and having to turn to a website that bombards you with junk just to look up a few simple opcodes and operands you’d better find a backup host before next month.

That said, Arm is willing to work something out with Palmisciano, the organization told us.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the team at WRITER is thrilled to announce the release of three newly introduced open models in the Palmyra-mini family. These models are designed to be powerful, lightweight, and highly performant for their size (1.5B to 1.7B), making them ideal for a wide range of applications with efficient inference.

The "thinking" models have been trained with a Chain of Thought (CoT) approach, which improves their reasoning abilities. We're excited to see what the community will build with these new models!

GGUF and MLX quantizations are also available for your convenience:.

palmyra-mini-thinking-a-MLX-BF16.

palmyra-mini-thinking-b-MLX-BF16.

palmyra-mini: Our non-reasoning improved base model, delivering a score of 52.6% on Big Bench Hard (get-answer)(exact_match), making it a fantastic all-rounder for a wide variety of generative tasks.

According to recent reports, palmyra-mini-thinking-a: This variant is your go-to for complex logical challenges. Trained with a Chain of Thought (CoT) approach, it achieves an impressive 82.87% on GSM8K (strict match), demonstrating its powerful reasoning capabilities. It has the highest overall average score on benchmarks relative to other models in the release.

Recent findings suggest that palmyra-mini-thinking-b: Pushing the boundaries of problem-solving, this model scores a solid 92.5% on AMC23. It's a great choice when you need a model that can "think" its way through demanding tasks. This has the highest average benchmark scores in the benchmarks AIME24,AIME25, GPQA, HMMT25, HLE, MMLU_PRO,MATH500, LCB relative to the other models in the release.

We're releasing both pass@1(avg-of-1) and pass@1(avg-of-64) results. Benchmarking methodology (sampling parameters: temperature 0.6, top_p 0.95): Pass@1(avg-of-1) scores:.

GSM8K through MBPP: collected using lm_eval framework. AIME24 through HMMT25: collected using lighteval framework.

Pass@1(avg-of-64) scores: collected using nemoskills framework.

Since all the base models are Qwen architecture the inference should be runnable on popular inference frameworks such as vLLM, SGLang, TRTLLM, TGI.

In a recent development, for palmyra-thinking-b the base model was https://huggingface.co/nvidia/OpenReasoning-Nemotron-1.5B. We ran RL fine tuning and observed that it's capable of improving performance. While Reinforcement learning improved single-shot accuracy (pass@1), it reduced sampling diversity, leading to a drop in majority@64 performance compared to the SFT base model. This highlights a trade-off between accuracy and diversity, and we believe transparency around these findings will spark further research along mode collapse, small model performance and other areas.

Through this work, we've tried to push the boundaries of what's achievable with small parameter models, and we're excited to see how the community will continue advancing inference efficiency without sacrificing performance quality.

#195140. The Next Insider Threat Will Be an Employee’s Personal AI Agent

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1531 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Unite ↗ Open Full Page

The Next Insider Threat Will Be an Employee’s Personal AI Agent

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1531 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Employees are connecting personal agents to work email and Slack faster than security can keep track.
  • Within the next year, employees’ personal AI agents will be working inside most large companies, and most security teams will not know which ones.
  • Sources indicate that the signal arrived in September.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Employees are connecting personal agents to work email and Slack faster than security can keep track. Four questions to help executives get ahead of it.

Within the next year, employees’ personal AI agents will be working inside most large companies, and most security teams will not know which ones.

Sources indicate that the signal arrived in September. Security researcher Patrick Wardle highlighted that malware on a Mac could take over a session of Meta’s upcoming Muse assistant and steer it across the victim’s devices. Muse works across files, email, messages and calendar, so whoever controls the session inherits all of it. Meta shipped a fix within a day.

According to recent reports, the flaw matters less than what it exposes. Most conversations about personal agents ask whether the agent is safe for the person using it. At work, the question changes. When an employee connects a personal agent to manufacturer email or Slack, it becomes an autonomous actor inside company systems that security never approved. It has an insider’s access and an insider’s credentials, and none of the controls companies apply to insiders: no background check, no security training, no offboarding. Companies built employee security around people, and the agent acting for each person gets no attention. I expect incidents like this to become routine in 2027.

Four questions separate the security teams in control from the ones guessing.

Which personal agents are already connected to work accounts?

It has been revealed that start here, because everything else depends on the answer. Shadow AI can account for more than 60% of an enterprise’s AI assets, and personal agents add to that share.

It has been revealed that in one deployment, a single employee machine had about 400 agent skills installed, and roughly half of them were malicious. The employee had not chosen them. They came bundled with an AI app installed for work. Public marketplaces show the same pattern: roughly 12% of the skills in one audit were malicious.

Many of these agents run on the desktop, where browser-based monitoring cannot see them. I see the same pattern in customer environments. A manufacturer blocks ChatGPT in the browser, so employees download the desktop app or use a personal account. I consider this the most underhyped blind spot in enterprise AI.

Blocking has also stopped being the default answer. A year ago, roughly nine out of ten of my customer conversations began with “we do not approve AI in our organization.” Today the question is how to enable employees safely, and that starts with an inventory. The cost of skipping it is documented: 92% of organizations with an AI-related breach lacked proper AI access controls.

If I had 90 days and one project, I would spend them here. Complete visibility across employee machines, desktops included, is a significant win on its own. In 2027, I expect personal agents to become as ordinary as the browser, so security has to follow the agent down to the individual employee: which agents each person runs, what those agents connect to and what they did.

Are approval and spending limits enforced outside the model?

“Ask me before you spend” is a request typed into the agent. It holds for as long as the agent honors it, and instructions can be forgotten, argued around or overwritten by an attacker.

The stronger design puts the limit outside the model. Even Meta designed Muse so that a separate component, outside the sandbox where the model runs, approves each request, and executives should expect the same arrangement for employee agents.

Sources indicate that tier the limits by risk. Low-risk, reversible actions such as reading a calendar can run automatically. Drafting a reply can run inside defined limits. Moving money, deleting data, sharing files externally and anything irreversible should wait for a person.

It has been revealed that requiring approval for everything creates fatigue and removes the value of the agent. A policy written into the task prompt also falls short. Runtime controls, enforced where the agent cannot edit them, have moved from nice to have to must-have. The industry calls the underlying risk excessive agency: more functionality, permission and autonomy than the task requires. As agents start booking, buying and paying in 2027, I expect transaction authorization to become a major concern. Approval will need to be tied to the specific payee and amount, not to a broad permission to spend granted months earlier.

There is a catch, and Muse reveals it too. Meta had this design in place, and the hijack still worked, because the attacker did not need to argue with the agent. It held the agent’s session. Limits outside the model govern what the agent may do. They cannot tell the agent apart from someone holding its keys. That is the job of identity.

Does every agent have its own identity?

If an agent signs in as the employee, every action looks like the employee took it. Investigators cannot tell whether the person or the agent sent a message, and the firm cannot switch off the agent without switching off the person. Shared credentials are one of the biggest violations I see.

It has been revealed that personal agents complicate this, because a tech giant cannot issue an identity to an agent an employee bought on a personal account. It does control the connection point. Access to company email and Slack runs through grants the company can see and govern, so it can require agents to connect through approved apps with their own scoped tokens, refuse connections that reuse the employee’s login and revoke any single grant without touching the employee’s account.

Sources indicate that A separate identity also answers the departure question. Companies have become reasonably good at cutting off access when an employee leaves, but only the access they know exists. An agent with its own identity can be revoked that day.

Scope matters as much, and the Muse flaw reveals why: one captured token carried everything the assistant was allowed to do. Read access to one Slack channel limits what a stolen token can do. Access to the whole workspace “just in case” sets the limit at everything.

According to recent reports, moving a credential into a secrets manager improves how it is stored and leaves its scope unchanged. Few teams revisit scope after the pilot, when a token minted for a two-week test quietly becomes the permission the agent runs on indefinitely.

Do you know what normal looks like?

Sources indicate that visibility, limits and identity reduce exposure, and they will not catch everything. Teams also need a baseline of how each agent normally behaves: which tools it uses, what data it touches and the order in which it acts. The baseline has to come from the tech giant’s own traffic, because normal for one organization’s agents looks nothing like normal for another’s.

Agent activity differs from human activity in ways a baseline can capture. A person pauses, second-guesses and goes deep on a few leads. An agent moves from reconnaissance to action almost immediately, keeps the same pace at step three and step three hundred, and probes many systems at once.

In a recent development, defenders hold an advantage here, because context is the one thing an attacking agent cannot shortcut. An attacker’s agent does not know which systems normally talk to each other or which data a given team touches, so it has to probe, and probing looks different from work. You do not need to catch the attack that works. You need to notice the looking.

Respond in steps. Watch the agent, flag it, slow it down, and block only when confident, with unclear cases going to a person. Trust in automated response also depends on explainability. If an analyst cannot see in plain language why an agent was flagged, they will never let automation act alone.

Personal agents will keep arriving, and employees will keep connecting them to the tools they use all day. The leaders who stay in control will find the agents first, enforce limits outside the model, give each agent an identity and learn what normal looks like.

Visibility comes first, and everything else follows from it.

How many personal agents are connected to your company’s email and Slack today? If the honest answer is a guess, that is where the first 90 days belong.

Ankita Gupta is the Co-founder and CEO of Akto, an enterprise Agentic AI Security and Governance platform helping organizations discover, monitor, and secure AI agents across their environments. She brings 15+ years of experience across cybersecurity, engineering, and enterprise technology, having held roles at JPMorgan, LinkedIn, and VMware. She works with Fortune 1000 enterprises to address emerging security challenges associated with AI adoption, autonomous agents, and the evolving AI threat landscape.

Inception, a upcoming data theft and extortion gang that security researchers have theorized is a rebrand of the ShinyHunters group, “reject[s] this attribution” and claims it has no affiliation with any prior cybercrime enterprise.

In a lengthy statement posted Tuesday and shared on X, the extortionists insist that they are a new group, with new operators, and that their alleged social engineering attacks aren’t copying anyone - but rather just abusing the weakest link in an organization’s security: “a human being holding a phone.”.

The rant follows a Monday report by Okta Threat Intelligence - along with social media speculation since Inception’s inception last week - that the newly emerged group is very likely ShinyHunters with a different name.

Okta’s researchers based their analysis on the two groups’ shared infrastructure, plus Inception’s nearly identical tactics: voice phishing, during which the scammers trick targets into entering credentials into phishing pages and approving multi-factor authentication (MFA) requests.

Industry observers note that inception apparently took offense to this. “We would like to address this once, clearly, and only once,” the crims' statement says. “We are not ShinyHunters. We were never ShinyHunters. We are Inception.”.

The gang argues that its overlapping domain registrars, hosting providers, and DNS services don’t prove anything. These are commodity services, “available to anyone who can pay for them,” Inception wrote.

Industry observers note that plus, their similar methodologies don't necessarily make Inception a reboot. “That is not theft of tradecraft,” they wrote. “It is acknowledgment of a good idea – the same way every group after LockBit used a leak site, and nobody called them LockBit.”.

“Inception is a new group, with new operators, our own objectives, and our own name,” the statement continues. “What we share with the past is plumbing.”.

To be fair, the newly introduced crime crew has every reason to distance itself from ShinyHunters.

That gang’s September FBI hack - plus several earlier digital heists during which the criminals stole information belonging to millions of people, including cancer patients, university and K-12 students - put a massive target on its collective backs.

And while at least three ShinyHunters suspects were arrested in September and October, there's no confirmation that authorities have dismantled the entire operation.

Plus, as a ShinyHunters spokesperson told The Register in an earlier interview, they and others in the crew started off as GnosticPlayers before rebranding as ShinyHunters in 2020 - so a reboot isn’t beyond the realm of possibility.

Inception, for its part, says it “will not comment further on the ghost of ShinyHunters,” and it has its own work to do. And by work, it means copying ShinyHunters' playbook, stealing corporate data, and extorting victim companies for massive sums of money.®.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Peptone announced on November 24, 2026 that its AI- and biophysics-developed prostate cancer candidate, PEP-5089, had entered Investigational New Drug (IND)-enabling development, the preclinical stage supporting an application to begin human trials. The organization also appointed Deepak Sampath as chief scientific officer.

Founder and chief executive Kamil Tamiola mentioned PEP-5089 moved from concept to candidate nomination in 18 months, including key in vivo experiments, and that the priority under Sampath’s scientific leadership is to advance the program toward Phase I.

PEP-5089 is an orally bioavailable small molecule that selectively targets the androgen receptor’s intrinsically disordered N-terminal domain, rather than the ligand-binding domain targeted by conventional anti-androgens. That distinction matters for AR-V7, a splice variant that lacks the ligand-binding domain but retains the region PEP-5089 is designed to inhibit.

Peptone reports that the candidate inhibited signaling from both full-length androgen receptor and AR-V7 in preclinical studies, retained activity against all six clinically relevant resistance variants in its ligand-binding-domain test panel, and inhibited tumor growth while substantially reducing prostate-specific antigen levels in prostate cancer xenograft models.

Peptone’s program page reports an unbound IC50 of 200 nM for PEP-5089 on its AR-V7 reporter assay, while approved comparators enzalutamide, apalutamide and darolutamide were inactive above 50,000 nM. These findings are preclinical and in vitro, and do not establish clinical benefit.

Sampath previously served as senior vice president and head of research at Ultragenyx after leadership roles at Genentech and Wyeth. His Peptone biography describes more than 25 years of experience across drug discovery, translational science, early development and regulatory submissions, including contributions to the discovery and development of the marketed oncology medicines venetoclax and inavolisib.

It has been revealed that across Ultragenyx, Genentech and Wyeth, he served as project or pharmacology leader for 16 programs that entered IND-enabling studies. Fourteen advanced into Phase I/II trials and six into Phase III, a record directly relevant to the development work Peptone is beginning for PEP-5089.

The manufacturer’s pipeline lists PEP-5089 as its only disclosed program in IND-enabling development. PEP-4212, a c-Myc antagonist for MYC-driven solid and liquid tumors, and PEP-3671, a TDP-43 aggregation modulator for ALS and frontotemporal dementia, remain in lead optimization.

Peptone pairs its AI models with experimental measurements of proteins in motion. The tech giant’s technology page describes ultra-fast hydrogen–deuterium exchange mass spectrometry, or HDX-MS: protein and heavy water are mixed in under 10 milliseconds, and the exchange reaction is quenched less than 50 milliseconds later, capturing hydrogen-exchange behavior associated with transient protein structure.

The instrument then fragments the protein and measures the small mass shifts caused by deuterium uptake. Software assembles the fragments into a map of structured and disordered regions over time and encodes that information for Peptone’s AI cluster. Conformational-sampling algorithms propose ensembles consistent with the measurements, exposing potential druggable sites in disordered proteins.

Tamiola said Peptone built its own hardware and developed proton–deuterium experiments specifically for disordered proteins: “These experiments generate unique data for our AI models, rather than leaving us dependent on existing datasets.”.

Together, the appointment and candidate nomination mark Peptone’s transition from platform-led discovery toward regulated drug development. The next substantive test is the IND-enabling work and, if PEP-5089 proceeds into patients, whether its reported preclinical activity translates into clinical benefit.

Industry News: Fund browser-grade certificate checking for every TLS client

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that non-browser applications have historically relied on a slowly changing set of trust roots maintained by the operating system or platform vendors.
  • The October 2026 eMudhra incident demonstrated the cost.
  • Sources indicate that upki ships these signals as a compact local cache that's updated automatically, independently of applications, so every TLS stack on a machine can share one copy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that non-browser applications have historically relied on a slowly changing set of trust roots maintained by the operating system or platform vendors. These trust roots are often based on browser root programs, but lack the data that allow browsers to make fine-grained trust decisions: revocation data for end entities, intermediates and roots (like CRLite and OneCRL), distrust dates and Certificate Transparency policy.

The October 2026 eMudhra incident demonstrated the cost. Browsers blocked the affected intermediates quickly, while other clients were unable to restrict only the affected intermediates. Instead, they had to wait for platform trust store updates to remove the parent root certificates and spent significant time and effort to mitigate the impact on their applications across different platforms and environments.

Sources indicate that upki ships these signals as a compact local cache that's updated automatically, independently of applications, so every TLS stack on a machine can share one copy. Its checks only ever narrow what a client accepts: they never make it trust a certificate it would otherwise reject.

It has been revealed that sponsorships are annual and pay for maintainer time on the roadmap and on ongoing maintenance. We don't sell individual features; priorities are open for discussion with sponsors.

For more information, contact Dirkjan Ochtman.

Sponsors help set priorities through quarterly roadmap calls.

Clients outside the browser accept revoked end-entity certificates.

upki syncs compact CRLite filters several times a day and checks revocation offline.

When root programs distrust a CA or intermediate, other clients keep trusting it until a trust store package update arrives, as the eMudhra incident indicated.

upki will ship OneCRL data, so distrust takes effect at the next cache patch.

Recent findings suggest that post-quantum signatures would add kilobytes to every TLS handshake. Merkle Tree Certificates can bring down the costs, but clients need landmarks delivered ahead of time to minimize handshake overhead.

upki will distribute landmarks alongside its other data.

Clients that don't enforce Certificate Transparency accept certificates that were never publicly logged, so misissuance can go unnoticed. Clients also don't benefit from certificate transparency logs blocking compromised/distrusted roots from obtaining proof of inclusion.

upki will deliver and maintain an up-to-date log list and policy inputs, so applications don't have to configure logs manually.

Servers that send an incomplete certificate chain work in browsers but fail verification in other clients.

upki will ship the known intermediate certificates, so clients can complete the chain as browsers do, without expensive network fetching.

Root changes, including private PKI roots, reach machines through OS packages or configuration management, which can be slow and uneven across a fleet.

upki's sync mechanism could distribute root sets to every machine.

The checks only protect applications whose TLS stack uses upki.

upki could gain native support in OpenSSL upstream, GnuTLS, NSS or in language runtimes.

Every check depends on data that's refreshed several times a day, on upstream sources and formats that keep changing, and on prompt fixes when security issues come up.

Sponsorship pays for releases, security response, dependency updates, keeping the data pipeline running and in step with upstream changes, supporting distribution packagers and maintaining C2SP specifications.

upki lives in the rustls organization on GitHub and is dual-licensed under Apache-2.0 and MIT.

Rahul Pangam, Co-Founder & CEO of RapidCanvas – Interview Series

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2549 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, rahul Pangam is Co-Founder and CEO of RapidCanvas, where he focuses on helping enterprises move AI applications from concept into production.
  • Sources indicate that rapidCanvas is a managed AI execution organization that combines an agentic AI platform with field AI engineers to develop and maintain enterprise applications.
  • Sources indicate that before co-founding RapidCanvas, you and Uttam Phalnikar built Simility, which was acquired by PayPal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, rahul Pangam is Co-Founder and CEO of RapidCanvas, where he focuses on helping enterprises move AI applications from concept into production. Before RapidCanvas, he co-founded Simility, which was acquired by PayPal. His work centers on building AI systems that fit real business workflows and remain useful as data, requirements, and operating conditions change.

Sources indicate that rapidCanvas is a managed AI execution organization that combines an agentic AI platform with field AI engineers to develop and maintain enterprise applications. Its approach brings together business context, reusable production infrastructure, and ongoing evaluation, with customers retaining ownership of their context, solution IP, and readable code.

Sources indicate that before co-founding RapidCanvas, you and Uttam Phalnikar built Simility, which was acquired by PayPal. What did that experience reveal about the challenges of deploying enterprise AI, and how did it shape your decision to start RapidCanvas?

Fraudsters change tactics the moment you catch them, so a model that was right last quarter can be wrong today. That’s the lesson Simility taught us about enterprise AI. Every customer had different data, risk tolerances and processes, and a wrong call cost real money. Most of our effort went into fitting the system to each customer’s workflow, capturing how their best analysts decided and giving the business enough visibility and control to trust it.

Sources indicate that A platform alone doesn’t make a market. You pick an urgent problem, prove value in production and expand from there. PayPal showed how much more valuable the technology became once it plugged into existing distribution and infrastructure.

Industry observers note that generative AI made prototypes cheap. Dependable business systems are still hard to build. RapidCanvas covers the full path from business problem to governed production application, so companies don’t have to choose between a tool they staff themselves and a consulting project that never repeats.

In a recent development, gartner predicts that 70% of enterprises will abandon agentic AI built by vendors’ forward-deployed engineers by 2028 because of rising costs and difficulty evolving those systems independently. RapidCanvas also pairs a platform with field AI engineers. What makes your approach different, and where do you agree with Gartner’s concerns?

According to recent reports, gartner has the failure mode right. When the field engineer becomes the product, the customer has bought dependency. The context and code sit with a few people outside the tech giant, and every change turns into a newly introduced engagement.

Our engineers have two jobs: capture the business context a generic platform can’t see, and turn repeated work into product. Each deployment should make the next one less custom. They start from reusable production infrastructure and domain patterns, and the customer’s definitions, rules, workflows and decision history live in an Enterprise Context Engine the customer owns.

Recent findings suggest that customers also own their solution IP and get readable code. They can run in their own cloud, a managed environment or SaaS, and nothing ties them to one model provider. We stay accountable after go-live without making the customer dependent on us. The test is whether the customer can see what the system knows, how it’s evaluated, what it’s allowed to do and how to change it. If the answer is no, Gartner’s concern is justified.

Industry observers note that you emphasize that your engineers remain accountable after applications go live. What does that accountability mean in practice when an application’s accuracy declines, business requirements change, or the expected financial return fails to materialize?

Too many vendors declare victory at go-live. That’s when our job really starts, because running software and valuable software are two different things.

It has been revealed that before launch, we agree with the customer on the business outcome and the technical bar. We test on their own data, set benchmarks with known answers and turn those criteria into a regression suite. After launch, we track accuracy, groundedness, human acceptance, errors, latency, cost and adoption. When performance slips, we diagnose the whole system before blaming the model. The cause could be data drift, a schema change, a latest business rule, a prompt, a model update or a workflow we never captured correctly. Every fix has to clear the same bar before users see it.

When the financial return doesn’t show up, the model, the workflow or the business hypothesis is wrong, and each calls for a different response. We might recalibrate, narrow the application’s authority, redesign the process, swap in conventional automation or stop the use case. Keeping a project alive because everyone is invested in it is the worst outcome. AI has to earn its place in the operation.

RapidCanvas offers custom AI applications through subscription pricing. How do you keep costs predictable as customers add integrations, increase usage and request changes, and what are the limits of what the subscription covers?

Predictable pricing comes from productizing the repeatable work and being upfront about what varies.

Customers pay a flat monthly subscription based on their exact needs. It covers customized solutions built with our experts, full platform access, user licenses, integrations, monitoring, maintenance, support and training. They can add or drop solutions and build new ones on the platform without opening a services project every time the business changes. That works because we reuse tested infrastructure and domain patterns, use deterministic software where it’s the better tool and route each task to the model with the right balance of accuracy, latency and cost.

It has been revealed that the price does assume a defined user population, deployment model, infrastructure footprint and support level. If a customer materially expands any of those, or moves into a upcoming data environment, we agree on the change before the economics shift. Normal evolution of an agreed solution stays in the subscription, while a materially new footprint is a commercial conversation. Customers should never see a change order for the routine work of keeping production AI useful.

Industry observers note that your Enterprise Context Engine captures business processes, rules and decision history. How do you turn undocumented employee knowledge into context an AI system can reliably use, particularly when people disagree about how a process should work?

Tribal knowledge only becomes usable context once it has a source, an owner and a decision rule. Dumping transcripts and documents into a large context window just creates a bigger pile of unstructured data.

According to recent reports, we start with what the organization already has: documents, system records, schemas, procedures and decision history. Then our engineers sit down with process owners and frontline employees to capture what those systems miss, including definitions, exceptions, approval paths and the reasons behind judgment calls. The Enterprise Context Engine turns all of it into structured, versioned context. Every fact traces back to a source, and every rule carries an owner and a change history.

It has been revealed that when people disagree, that tells you the process was never standardized. The system surfaces the conflict, and we work out whether it reflects a legitimate variation by region, product or business unit or whether the company needs one approved rule. A named process owner decides, and we record the decision, exceptions, effective date and approval. Until the business resolves it, the AI shouldn’t pretend it has. That call stays with a person.

How do you decide whether a customer’s problem needs an autonomous agent, a predictive model or conventional automation? Can you share an example where a simpler approach proved more effective than an agentic system?

The most mature AI architecture usually has less AI than people expect. Each approach should do the job it’s best at.

Recent findings suggest that conventional software or rules should carry most of the load when the logic is stable, repeatable and explainable. A predictive model may be enough when the business needs a forecast, score or probability. Agents make sense for workflows that involve multiple steps, changing information, tool use and judgment within clear limits. Most serious applications combine all three, with people keeping authority over the highest-stakes decisions.

In a recent development, invoice reconciliation shows why. One customer had to reconcile invoices across 15 entities and eight currencies. Most of that work called for normalization, matching logic and consistent rules. AI added value on the ambiguous cases, and people reviewed the exceptions. The application went live in three months and now matches more than 90% of invoices automatically. A fully autonomous agent would have added variance to a process that depends on exactness. The goal is the best business outcome with the least unnecessary complexity.

In a recent development, reusing components across deployments can improve economics, but each business has different requirements. Which parts of an AI solution can you safely standardize, and how do you validate that a component proven for one customer will work for another?

Standardize the scaffolding and leave the judgment to the customer. Every enterprise application needs production engineering, and very little of it is unique to any one tech giant.

Sources indicate that we standardize authentication, role-based access control, data connectors, deployment, audit logging, security scanning, monitoring, testing, error handling and the evaluation harness. We also reuse domain patterns for recurring problems like invoice reconciliation, document extraction and forecasting. That gives every engineer a real head start.

What stays customer-specific is the business context: terminology, data shape, thresholds, approval hierarchy, exceptions, risk tolerance and outcome measures. We treat reuse as a hypothesis. A component that worked for one customer gets us to validation faster but never lets us skip it. Every deployment is tested on the customer’s own data against acceptance criteria for that workflow, including edge cases, access controls, security, load and end-to-end behavior. Reuse shortens the time it takes to produce evidence, and the evidence bar stays where it was.

What testing and monitoring should an enterprise require before allowing an AI application to take consequential actions? How do you handle model updates, unexpected behavior and decisions that need human approval?

Autonomy is a delegation decision before it’s a model decision. Companies already have rules for delegating authority to people, and AI needs the same discipline.

Before an application takes a consequential action, the company should define what the system can see, what it can recommend, what it can do on its own and what needs approval. Each task type needs an acceptance threshold, examples from the customer’s own data and a trace from every output back to its source, rules and model. The application also needs access controls, end-to-end and load testing, a named owner, an audit trail and a rollback path.

In high-stakes workflows, recommending and acting should be separate steps. Payments, claims, regulated decisions, material financial commitments and unusual exceptions go to a person until the evidence supports more autonomy. Model updates should be handled like software releases, with any new model, prompt or schema change clearing the same regression suite first. If behavior turns unexpected, the system should stop or narrow its actions, route the case to review and roll back if needed. Autonomy gets earned one workflow at a time and stays revocable.

RapidCanvas states more than 40% of its customers now run multiple AI use cases in production. Could you walk us through a customer’s progression from its first deployment to broader adoption, including measurable results and anything that did not work as expected?

In a recent development, that 40% is the number I watch most closely. A successful pilot is good evidence, but the real proof is a customer asking for a second and third use case because the first one changed how the business runs. Here’s what that looks like in practice.

Recent findings suggest that one North American channel incentive management platform started with claims processing. We captured the rules behind the workflow and built controlled paths to approve, hold, adjust or reject each claim. The decision engine now applies 499 business rules and has processed more than 11,000 claims. In one recent quarter it adjudicated 494 claims, approving 297, declining 77 invalid ones and holding 84 for review.

Industry observers note that once that workflow was stable and the customer could see how decisions were made, the relationship grew to four use cases across claims adjudication, program intake and fraud mitigation. Each new one started with the context, controls and infrastructure the first had already established.

It has been revealed that not everything moved at the same pace. The fraud work stayed in design longer because the outcome definition and telemetry weren’t ready, and we had no results we were comfortable claiming. I’d rather delay a use case than automate something we can’t yet evaluate. A good first deployment doesn’t make every neighboring process ready for AI.

Industry observers note that as AI automates more application development, how will the role of field AI engineers change? What expertise should enterprises retain internally so they can understand, govern and eventually modify their systems without becoming dependent on a vendor?

It has been revealed that code is getting cheaper, which makes judgment worth more. Field AI engineers will write less of the undifferentiated foundation and spend more time understanding the business, choosing the architecture, defining evaluations, designing exception paths and setting controls.

Industry observers note that the role moves toward architect, adviser and validator, and the technical work becomes more consequential. The key skill is knowing where AI belongs, where deterministic software does better, what evidence to require and how the system should behave when it’s uncertain. The strongest engineers will translate between domain experts, data, software and governance, with no single model at the center.

Enterprises don’t need to build an AI lab, but they should keep the expertise a model can’t replace. That means a business or product owner accountable for the outcome, domain owners who know the exceptions, data and architecture leadership, security, risk and compliance expertise and enough engineering skill to inspect the code, integrations, configuration, evaluations and change history. The customer should own the durable assets: its context, solution IP, readable code, evaluation suite and change-control record. A good partner leaves the enterprise more capable after every deployment and never becomes indispensable.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is taking heat from AI luminary Yann LeCun, one of the founding fathers of modern machine learning, because of the Claudefather's fear-mongering around open-weights models, which also happen to compete with his products.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

‘It’s like the Ottoman Empire banning the printing press for Arabic so they would keep in control of the dogma,’ he states.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is taking heat from AI luminary Yann LeCun, one of the founding fathers of modern machine learning, because of the Claudefather's fear-mongering around open-weights models, which also happen to compete with his products.

In an X post this week, LeCun likened the Amodei's advocacy to a “upcoming form of medieval obscurantism.”.

“Dario’s spiel since GPT-2 has always been about hyping the dangers so that open models would be made illegal, and he would stay in control,” LeCun wrote in response to a now three-year-old video posted to the platform in which Amodei warned US Congress members about the dangers of open-weights models, the use of which could not be monitored or policed.

In a recent development, “He left OpenAI because he wasn’t going to have control. It’s like the Ottoman Empire banning the printing press for Arabic so they would keep in control of the dogma.”.

LeCun is one of the most influential names in AI and ML. His team is credited with the development of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in the late ’80s during his time at Bell Labs. He later oversaw the development of Meta’s Llama herd of models as chief AI scientist before shifting gears away from LLMs to world model architectures like JEPA. He has also been a strong proponent of open source AI development and open models.

Of the major model houses, Anthropic has taken the most hostile position against the adoption of open-weights models.

Despite advocating against the unregulated diffusion of open models for years, Anthropic’s fearmonger-in-chief has maintained that the company isn’t opposed to them. “Anthropic has never advocated for a ban on open-weights models,” Amodei wrote in a blog post earlier this year.

The executive has instead fomented fears over their potential misuse.

“Open-weights models — it does not matter whether they come from China or anywhere else — do potentially present a higher risk than closed models, because it is very difficult to apply guardrails to them or monitor their usage, and, once weights are released, they cannot be withdrawn,” the blog post read.

Amodei has repeatedly hammered these talking points over the past several years, including in the Senate hearing that solicited LeCun’s post.

Amodei has also called for measures, such as stricter export controls on the export of high-end accelerators to China; a crackdown on industrial-scale distillation operations, for which his manufacturer has previously accused Alibaba and other Chinese model devs; and mandating safety testing for sufficiently advanced open-weights models.

In other words, Anthropic doesn’t want all freely downloadable models banned, just the ones that Amodei thinks aren’t playing fair or are powerful enough to compete with its own.

LeCun isn’t the only one who has pushed back against anti-open-weights rhetoric in recent memory.

Earlier this summer, a cadre of tech titans, including Meta, Microsoft, IBM, Dell, and Nvidia, wrote an open letter [PDF] in support of open-weights models.

Open models “strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable sovereignty,” Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang noted at the time. “The world needs both frontier closed models and frontier open models.”.

As we previously reported, Nvidia’s future depends on its ability to sell to a diverse set of customers ranging from the massive model houses like Anthropic and OpenAI to public clouds, neoclouds, and enterprises. And while many of these companies are perfectly happy to get their AI through Claude or ChatGPT, others, whether it be for regulatory or cost reasons, are not.

Earlier this month, we reported how British neobank Revolut cut their vibe coding tab by 10x by moving its roughly 2,000 employees from Claude to Z.AI’s GLM 5.1 running on a cluster of 56 Nvidia B200 GPUs.

The problem for Anthropic, and OpenAI for that matter, is the more enterprises that embrace open-weights models, the less likely they are to spring for Claude or ChatGPT.

The Register reached out to Anthropic for comment, but had not heard back at the time of publication. ®.

Sources indicate that TL;DR Today we release LeRobotDataset:v3! In our previous LeRobotDataset:v2 release, we stored one episode per file, hitting file-system limitations when scaling datasets to millions of episodes. LeRobotDataset:v3 packs multiple episodes in a single file, using relational metadata to retrieve information at the individual episode level from multi-episode files. The fresh format also natively supports accessing datasets in streaming mode, allowing to process large datasets on the fly.We provide a one-liner util to convert all datasets in the LeRobotDataset format to the new format, and are very excited to share this milestone with the community ahead of our next stable release!

LeRobotDataset is a standardized dataset format designed to address the specific needs of robot learning, and it provides unified and convenient access to robotics data across modalities, including sensorimotor readings, multiple camera feeds and teleoperation status. Our dataset format also stores general information regarding the way the data is being collected (metadata), including a textual description of the task being performed, the kind of robot used and measurement details like the frames per second at which both image and robot state streams are sampled. Metadata are useful to index and search across robotics datasets on the Hugging Face Hub!

Within lerobot, the robotics library we are developing at Hugging Face, LeRobotDataset provides a unified interface for working with multi-modal, time-series data, and it seamlessly integrates both with the Hugging Face and Pytorch ecosystems. The dataset format is designed to be easily extensible and customizable, and already supports openly available datasets from a wide range of embodiments—including manipulator platforms such as the SO-100 arms and ALOHA-2 setup, real-world humanoid data, simulation datasets, and even self-driving car data! You can explore the current datasets contributed by the community using the dataset visualizer! 🔗.

Besides scale, this new release of LeRobotDataset also enables support for a streaming functionality, allowing to process batches of data from large datasets on the fly, without having to download prohibitively large collections of data onto disk. You can access and use any dataset in v3.0 in streaming mode by using the dedicated StreamingLeRobotDataset interface! Streaming datasets is a key milestone towards more accessible robot learning, and we are excited about sharing it with the community 🤗.

It has been revealed that lerobot is the end-to-end robotics library developed at Hugging Face, supporting real-world robotics as well as state of the art robot learning algorithms. The library allows to record datasets locally directly on real-world robots, and to store datasets on the Hugging Face Hub. You can read more about the robots we currently support here!

Head to the official documentation to see how to record a dataset for your use case.

A core design choice behind LeRobotDataset is separating the underlying data storage from the user-facing API. This allows for efficient serialization and storage while presenting the data in an intuitive, ready-to-use format. Datasets are organized into three main components:.

In a recent development, to support datasets with potentially millions of episodes (resulting in hundreds of millions/billions of individual frames), we merge data from different episodes into the same high-level structure. Concretely, this means that any given tabular collection and video will not contain information about one episode only, but a concatenation of the information available in multiple episodes. This keeps the pressure on the file system manageable, both locally and on remote storage providers like Hugging Face. We can then leverage metadata to gather episode-specific information, e.g. the timestamp a given episode starts or ends in a certain video.

Every dataset on the Hugging Face Hub containing the three main pillars presented above (Tabular and Visual Data, as well as relational Metadata), and can be accessed with a single line.

According to recent reports, most robot learning algorithms, based on reinforcement learning (RL) or behavioral cloning (BC), tend to operate on a stack of observations and actions. For instance, RL algorithms typically use a history of previous observations o_{t-H_o:t}, and BC algorithms are instead typically trained to regress chunks of multiple actions. To accommodate for the specifics of robot learning training, LeRobotDataset provides a native windowing operation, whereby we can use the seconds before and after any given observation using a delta_timestamps argument.

Conveniently, by using LeRobotDataset with a PyTorch DataLoader one can automatically collate the individual sample dictionaries from the dataset into a single dictionary of batched tensors.

You can also use any dataset in v3.0 format in streaming mode, without the need to download it locally, by using the StreamingLeRobotDataset class.

LeRobotDataset v3.0 is a stepping stone towards scaling up robotics datasets supported in LeRobot. By providing a format to store and access large collections of robot data we are making progress towards democratizing robotics, allowing the community to train on possibly millions of episodes without even downloading the data itself!

You can try the new dataset format by installing the latest lerobot-v0.3.x, and share any feedback on GitHub or on our Discord server! 🤗.
