📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Meta added its Muse personal AI agent to Instagram direct messages on November 24, 2026, announcing through Muse’s verified Instagram account that people can send it a DM to “turn your saves into real plans,” with a trip they have been meaning to take as the example.

The addition gives Muse a conversational entry point inside Instagram alongside its other chat surfaces. Meta’s Muse product site describes chatting through the Muse app on mobile or desktop, or directly in WhatsApp, by message or voice. It separately lists Instagram among the apps that can be connected to the agent, with consumers deciding what Muse can see and do.

In its September 8, 2026 launch post, Meta said Muse could organize Instagram Saves and create artifacts such as travel guides from them, with Instagram connected as one source of context. The initial standalone rollout was in the US on iOS, Android and the Muse website.

That workflow reflects Muse’s intended difference from a conventional chatbot. Meta describes the agent as remembering conversations, proactively working toward goals and suggesting ideas, rather than only answering isolated questions. The DM entry point connects task initiation with the place where the content was saved. For Meta, the product significance is a shift from Instagram as a source of context to Instagram as both a source and a place to delegate work.

Sources indicate that meta’s account infrastructure already links some of these services. Its connector documentation states Facebook, Instagram and Threads connect automatically when the accounts share an Accounts Center. While connected, Muse exchanges information relevant to the tasks assigned to it. Consumers can manage those accounts through Accounts Center.

Sources indicate that private-message access has a more specific boundary. Meta’s security and privacy page states Muse does not read private messages unless the user grants access through private-messaging connectors or Muse on Mac. Permissions are set per connector, and customers can read, edit or delete what Muse remembers. The upcoming DM surface lets someone message Muse; it does not, by itself, alter that documented rule for reading private messages.

Actions beyond retrieving information carry another set of controls. Meta’s approval guide distinguishes read actions, such as checking a calendar or reading an email, from write actions, such as sending a message or making a purchase. People can require approval before every write action and notable read actions, or before any action, and inspect a chronological activity log. Some actions can be stopped or undone in chat, but a sent email cannot be reversed.

According to recent reports, disconnecting a connector stops future data exchanges, but information previously used for tasks may remain in Muse’s memories and conversation history. The data-control guide notes stored interactions can include text, voice, photos and information obtained through connectors. Deleting material also does not necessarily erase information Muse learned from it.

Recent findings suggest that owners can delete individual messages and side chats, ask Muse to forget a topic or set of interactions, or reset the agent to permanently delete its chat history, files and active tasks. The setting allowing interactions to help train Meta’s AI models is on initially, and turning it off also applies to previous interactions. The result is a more direct route from saved Instagram content to delegated work, with permissions and retention settings determining how far that delegation extends.

#195129. Bypassing iOS Safari 60 FPS Limit

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2186 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rida ↗ Open Full Page

Bypassing iOS Safari 60 FPS Limit

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2186 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rida

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Devon Govett of React Aria posted “Scrolling is All You Need: Building a Swipeable Sheet” back in October, and in it he talked about his team developing a sheet component that cleverly leverages the physics and smooth interactions provided by native browsers to provide the illusion of a native interaction.
  • In a recent development, more recently, Jordan Walke, creator of React, posted a video of an experiment on X showing a convincing native-like mobile interaction using DOM & CSS.
  • It has been revealed that what the video Jordan Walke posted doesn’t show is that, unless you flip the “Prefer Page Rendering Updates near 60fps” flag buried deep within the Safari developer settings on iOS, WebKit limits requestAnimationFrame to just 60 Hz on a 120 Hz screen, and on a regular page, touch and pointer events are held to that same rate.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rida F'kih · November 20, 2026 · 10 min read.

Devon Govett of React Aria posted “Scrolling is All You Need: Building a Swipeable Sheet” back in October, and in it he talked about his team developing a sheet component that cleverly leverages the physics and smooth interactions provided by native browsers to provide the illusion of a native interaction.

In a recent development, more recently, Jordan Walke, creator of React, posted a video of an experiment on X showing a convincing native-like mobile interaction using DOM & CSS. It re-established a long-lived itch that I’ve had, and prompted this response from me. It’s something I could never justify building, however. Anything I built using this method would be pegged to 60 FPS.

It has been revealed that what the video Jordan Walke posted doesn’t show is that, unless you flip the “Prefer Page Rendering Updates near 60fps” flag buried deep within the Safari developer settings on iOS, WebKit limits requestAnimationFrame to just 60 Hz on a 120 Hz screen, and on a regular page, touch and pointer events are held to that same rate. This is what makes even the best mobile websites feel irritating to use.

Sources indicate that how can I make this experience suck less without resorting to flags? Let’s call back to the React Aria piece. The reason it feels so nice is that scrolling is the responsibility of the compositor. It runs in its own thread. It moves, clips and fades without a JavaScript round-trip.

Sources indicate that finger to digitizer, digitizer to compositor, compositor to GPU. This will become the basis of our interaction.

Behold, two grids. They both move a square when you drag. The one on the left uses JavaScript events and sets the transform attribute in CSS, while the one on the right simply places a square in a scrollable area.

If you’re on iOS Safari, you’ll immediately be able to tell which is which because one refreshes at most 60 times a second in a renderer pass, while the other uses the compositor.

According to recent reports, in order to leverage the power of the scroll area, we need to find a way to read the scroll position outside of the renderer. If we can do that, we can treat it like a trackpad, or use it to “extract” native bounce, physics, momentum, etc., and apply them directly from the compositor to our animations.

The point is, it’d be crazy flexible if we could just find a way to pull the values out of it frequently enough.

I measured scroll events updating 5 to 26 times per second during momentum scroll on an iPhone Duo. The best-case scenario is during slow, deliberate scrolls where it reaches almost 60 updates a second. Useless.

Instead, we’ll be aiming to read scrollTop and scrollLeft synchronously.

Sources indicate that first, I tried having a MessageChannel call itself recursively, which worked: but it produced 50,000 reads a second with just 80 distinct values. That’s a lot of waste and heat since it pins a CPU core.

Next failure was trying to use Atomics to wake at the screen’s refresh rate, which worked and similarly extracted 80 distinct positions every second, but the drawbacks were too great. Since it needs a SharedArrayBuffer, we’re forced to use COOP/COEP headers which break cross-origin assets on our website.

Sources indicate that what finally worked was using a MessageChannel like before, throttling the next measurement to the next tick using a setTimeout according to the refresh rate of the device, phase-locked to vsync using requestAnimationFrame timestamps. I was nervous about this approach, but as you’ll see later, it panned out well. The only remaining drawback specific to this solution was easy to work around. iOS rounds performance.now() to the millisecond, so I derived the minimum time between draws from the refresh interval.

In a recent development, each solution got us 80 position reads per second. Two-thirds towards our goal of 120 Hz input.

Safari’s UI process sends the web process one scroll position at a time, and waits for an acknowledgement from the web process before sending another. Anything that arrives in the meantime is overwritten. This was costing us dropped positions. Digging through WebKit yielded what we needed to get around this. It turns out that on every tick where the page has a rendering enhancement queued, Safari flushes the position without waiting. An empty requestAnimationFrame loop is all we need to do that.

This bought us ~12.5% more reads, and brought us to 90 unique position reads per second.

I sort of assumed I had hit the limit of the aforementioned IPC, but it turns out that ProMotion was just deciding that there’s no need to render at a refresh rate higher than 90 Hz.

Squeezing out the last 30 Hz was trickier. A GPU-accelerated CSS animation lets the screen go to 120 Hz, but only while something is scrolling. So a tiny invisible scroller smooth-scrolls in the background, ready to boost us to the full ProMotion refresh rate whenever we need it.

Of course, we don’t want the display pegging to 120 Hz the entire time, so we reserve all the tricks we used to get there for times we expect animations to occur: touch events, scroll-derived animations, etc.

If the interaction you’re building doesn’t need momentum, rubber banding, or snapping, you can forego them entirely and just use a passive touchmove listener on the controller which fires at the full 120 Hz.

Industry observers note that just like that, we’re receiving updates from the controller at a full 120 Hz! Drag the grid below to see.

According to recent reports, one issue remains. scrollTop and scrollLeft are rounded to the nearest integer even though iOS scrolls with sub-point precision. Easy fix, thankfully. We just scale the scrollable surface up by the device pixel ratio, then its container back down by its reciprocal.

If you want to use the viewport itself as a controller, you can choose to invasively set the initial-scale in the same way, but this comes with some caveats. You’ll have to scale units by the DPR, disable text autosizing, and manually scale safe areas. You’ll also get tiny text-selection indicators. All trade-offs, but by no means required.

Sources indicate that from here on out, I’ll refer to these scrolling grids as “controllers”, because they act exactly like one. All we have to do is make one invisible and lay it over where we want to read high-frequency input.

Note that the page itself can also be a controller, but Safari will throttle reported scroll positions to 10 Hz during the URL bar resize that happens when you change scroll direction. WebKit skips this if we give the page a scroll-driven animation that animates a non-GPU-accelerated attribute. I went with transitioning between two transparent colours for this page.

In a recent development, now we get high-frequency input, but the DOM still only updates 60 times a second, so if we tried to leverage it as it stands, we’d just be updating a value twice for every frame that’s drawn. The user would get no benefit.

The vast majority of dragging interactions are already covered by our controllers, and predefined animations are covered by CSS animations. But what about more complicated interactions? What about computation-derived layouts? What about shaders?

In a recent development, ask your search engine or AI of choice today “How to render canvas content on iOS at 120 Hz without feature flag?” and it will respond that this is a fundamental impossibility in iOS Safari. Even WebKit’s own bug tracker is full of people asking for it. Ink & Switch, game-engine makers. People even cite Capacitor & Tauri as resorting to private APIs.

Asking Google yields the following preamble.

There is no public web API or standard JavaScript workaround to force HTML5 (requestAnimationFrame) to run at 120 Hz on iOS Safari without changing the system feature flag.

Fable 5.2 shares the same sentiment.

Short answer: you can't, for JavaScript-drawn canvas frames. On iOS, WebKit caps page rendering updates (which is when canvas content is presented) at 60 Hz unless the user turns off the flag. No web API overrides it. […] Timer-based loops (setTimeout, MessageChannel) won't help, in my understanding: you can draw more often, but the result is still presented at the 60 Hz rendering update. Low Power Mode throttles further.

At first, I tunnel-visioned on scroll. I tried breaking workers, pre-rendering permutation “flip-books,” and even live-generating video. It was all too laggy, jagged, or required so much RAM the WebKit process just crashed.

Seven attempts later, and a whole lot of agents digging through WebKit’s source, I landed on this.

According to recent reports, in WebKit on iOS, if we create a canvas element and call transferControlToOffscreen, we get an OffscreenCanvas back. The original canvas element becomes a placeholder, and WebKit (following the HTML specification’s recommendation) skips waiting for the next rendering pass when an OffscreenCanvas pushes a frame.

Unlike earlier attempts, without workarounds this is easy on the battery and only uses as much memory as is needed to support a higher-frequency backing store.

According to recent reports, jackpot. We now have 120 FPS rendering on iOS WebKit canvases.

Now we can take any input at 120 Hz, and render an output at that very same frame rate. The first thing I created for this was a small UI clone of Ando’s mobile application fitted with a Liquid Glass tab bar, buttons, and buttery smooth navigation interactions. Once installed as a PWA, I kept having to double-take to check I wasn’t in the native application.

According to recent reports, this page is fitted with two custom “Liquid Glass” elements in the viewport. Each of them renders at the full device refresh rate. We have to be very deliberate in order to do this in a way that is performant and convincing.

Industry observers note that when the page first loads, we take a snapshot and load it into a WebGL texture. This texture is used as the foundation for a composite that is then fed into our shader.

It has been revealed that as the page scrolls, we then sample the region beneath each component, which is all we need to produce our effect. Building it this way means that no matter how the content below it is built, it can decide the best way to keep the texture live.

Sources indicate that on this page, components using requestAnimationFrame for illustrative reasons update the texture from the main thread. Components using OffscreenCanvas post their frames directly from their workers to the worker managing the texture. This keeps us off the main thread and lets us get shaders refreshing at 120 Hz.

After all that, the glass just samples a small region around where it would land on the composite texture and computes the frame.

Let’s build our Liquid Glass tab bar. We’ll start out by just drawing the underlying structure.

In a recent development, we’ll break this down into one controller for each button. Each controller sends us timestamped events: which controller is being used, and how much it has been dragged. We keep a short history of those samples, so we know when a press has moved far enough to count as a drag, and how fast the finger is moving. Nothing else. Everything else is derived from that.

We now build a state machine around this. Every frame, the upcoming events go in, and a frame comes out: where the lens is, how far it has lifted and stretched, and how visible the pill is.

Finally, we apply some shaders to get a convincing Liquid Glass effect.

Industry observers note that I built a benchmark environment and recorded an iPhone 18 Pro at 240 FPS, slowing it down to an eighth to benchmark the difference. The two oscillating squares measure inputs and renders.

Over three seconds of dragging, the controller version averaged 118 FPS while the pointer events version held a steady 60. Even in Low Power Mode, which traditionally limits you to 30, this approach gets you 60.

In a recent development, liquid Glass was the target as an overblown example, but this unlocks a lot. For the first time, you can take input and render output at true device-native speeds on iOS Safari. Micro-interactions feel native and delightful, PWAs which ignored the aforementioned feature flag finally have a way to render at 120 Hz, and look at all the fun we had along the way!

Recent findings suggest that would I rebuild my entire application around this? No. Fact remains it’s completely within Apple’s rights and would not violate the HTML specification if they just decided to make OffscreenCanvas’ placeholder wait for the main thread rendering pass. They even have a strong track record of “party pooping” as was done shortly after Lochie Axon unveiled the web-haptics library. I’d much prefer they make these findings moot by disabling the feature flag and natively supporting ProMotion for websites, but Apple is Apple for a reason after all.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, google declared on November 24, 2026 that its Workspace Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and Workspace command-line interface (CLI) are generally available, alongside rules requiring AI agents to use those interfaces instead of existing REST APIs. Technical enforcement begins February 1, 2027.

Google reports that Workspace APIs handle more than 2.8 trillion calls a month, with public Drive API traffic more than two-and-a-half times its 2022 volume. Traditional applications can continue using existing REST APIs; the new requirement applies to AI agents and other AI-driven tools.

Google’s rationale is that traditional REST APIs were built for human-paced applications, where a valid OAuth token implied user intent. An autonomous agent acting at machine speed across email, documents and cloud infrastructure changes that assumption. The upcoming design puts policy checks, data boundaries and human confirmation into the request path.

Sources indicate that the Workspace servers use MCP to give AI applications a standard way to read data and take actions. Dedicated remote servers are generally available for Gmail, Drive, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Calendar, Chat and Tasks, inheriting each user’s permissions and data-governance controls. The Workspace CLI serves local agents, terminal workflows and automation, with structured JSON output and scoped OAuth sign-in across Workspace services.

Recent findings suggest that each agent call through these interfaces is checked against organizational permissions, data-loss-prevention rules and classification labels. The MCP servers reject OAuth clients that are not designated for AI agents, and agents connecting to Workspace must use dedicated OAuth client IDs with least-privilege scopes and usage quotas. Billing is scheduled to begin on April 1, 2027, while time-limited approvals are listed as coming soon.

In a recent development, draft creation and document summarization can run autonomously. Sending email, changing Drive sharing permissions and making bulk edits require explicit user confirmation. Workspace administrators can view, audit and revoke agents in the admin console; user-facing activity review and revocation, plus controls to block agent access to Gmail messages and specific Drive files or folders, remain forthcoming.

Recent findings suggest that the Workspace AI Tools Addendum covers standalone agents, the software harnesses that deploy or orchestrate them, and applications or services using AI models. It bars disguising a tool to avoid classification or circumvent the Google MCP requirement. That makes the migration a compliance glitch for third-party agent platforms as well as for developers building directly on Workspace.

Recent findings suggest that workspace user data and Google Technical Information, a category of service information obtained or derived through Workspace access points, may be processed only to fulfill active, user-authorized tasks. Neither category can be used for model training, fine-tuning, evaluation dataset construction, model distillation or developing a service similar to a Workspace service. Scraping and systematic probing beyond what an authorized task requires are also prohibited.

Google Technical Information cannot be stored for more than 30 days. Covered user data and technical information must not be retained after a tool is disconnected or its access is revoked. If Google reasonably believes those rules have been violated, it can immediately restrict or remove the tool’s access, or suspend or terminate the customer’s access to the relevant Workspace services.

On Google Cloud, Agent Gateway verifies Agent Identities against the Agent Registry directory, enforces identity and access management policies and default-deny outbound rules, and screens requests with Model Armor. It governs inbound client-to-agent traffic and outbound requests from agents to tools, APIs and other agents. Custom authorization checks can be delegated to an organization’s own policy engine or third-party security tools through Service Extensions.

Industry observers note that cloud Run support and Agent Gateway for cross-cloud Kubernetes environments remain in Limited Preview. Each gateway instance can govern up to 5,000 resources registered in Agent Registry.

Google’s MCP configuration guide requires screening prompts and responses for indirect prompt injection, meaning hidden instructions in untrusted content, using Model Armor or a documented alternative. Malicious emails or documents could hijack a session and modify, steal or delete data. Current known issues include some English-only approval prompts, no user self-service viewing or revocation of saved tool approvals, and expiration of those approvals after 90 days.

For enterprises, agent governance is now built into the supported Workspace access path. The practical burden is the migration: existing agent integrations must satisfy the new identity, confirmation, screening and retention rules on Google’s schedule, while parts of the user-control and deployment model remain pending.

Beyond Linux: A Journey Through the Open Source Ecosystem

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 24 min read (4813 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dragas

⏱️ ~24 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • What follows is the text of the talk I gave at Linux Day 2026 in Modena, lightly adapted for the blog.
  • Industry observers note that linux is one of the best-known players in the open source world, but it's not the only possible path.
  • According to recent reports, my name is Stefano Marinelli.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What follows is the text of the talk I gave at Linux Day 2026 in Modena, lightly adapted for the blog. The talk was in Italian, in front of a Linux audience - which explains a few of the jokes.

Industry observers note that linux is one of the best-known players in the open source world, but it's not the only possible path. A journey through the BSDs, illumos and other alternative operating systems, to reflect on Open Source as an idea, a philosophy and a practice of sharing knowledge.

According to recent reports, my name is Stefano Marinelli. I'm a sysadmin and consultant, and I run my own small company specialised in open source services and solutions. I like to call myself the "Barista" of the BSD Cafe and the illumos Cafe, online communities of people passionate about technology, open source and sharing. Today I'm not here just to talk about operating systems, but about freedom, sharing and knowledge. From free software to open source.

My first contact with the Free Software world was in 1996, when I wasn't even 17 yet. I saw a box set advertised in a magazine: "a whole operating system, for free", at a very low price. Something like 30,000 lire. Shortly before, I'd paid roughly ten times as much for the Windows 95 upgrade edition. Dismissive and without a shred of trust, I decided to order it and give it a go. I mean: who would ever write something like that... and release the source code? But six CDs for 30,000 lire... let's try. Worst case, it'll be an experience.

Sources indicate that it was love at first shell. That terminal opened up a whole universe, and to what I already knew (commercial licences, freeware, shareware) I added the concept of Free Software. But I didn't have enough hardware to run two operating systems, so I reinstalled Windows and put it all off. Still, I started thinking. Reflecting. Studying. In 1997 I got a new PC and started using Linux - or, as I was careful to say, GNU/Linux - for everything. Except games. For those, a small Windows partition survived, though not for long.

Sources indicate that in 1998 I enrolled in Computer Science at the University of Bologna. Even back then, it was a faculty strongly oriented towards free software. Linux in the labs. I was one of the few who, in the first year, already knew what Free Software was (not free as in price, but...freedom!) and how to use the Linux workstations. That gave me a massive advantage, especially from the second year onwards. Renzo Davoli was already pushing hard in that direction. I decided that would be my path. And so it was, and I started pushing too. Windows wasn't the "enemy" to me. The imposition was. Personally, I respect rules, but not impositions. Some people followed me, others watched from a distance. I didn't care. I was widening my horizons.

Sources indicate that in the early 2000s I also discovered the BSDs. And I convinced my parents that I needed a laser printer for "university material". In reality, I wanted to print the excellent BSD documentation. Maybe not university material, but the printed FreeBSD Handbook probably served me better than half of the theory exams I took back then. Thanks, mom and dad!

But let's get back to the beginning.

Free Software was born out of a change. In those days, code circulated freely among people. Depending on their needs, they exchanged source code, modified it and shared it again. But at some point this began to change. There's an anecdote that, while not exhaustive, gives the idea: the printer Richard Stallman was using kept jamming, and nobody got notified. He wanted to modify the software so that he'd get a notification, as he'd done with the previous printer. Back then it was common practice, but this time he was refused. "I can't share the source code. It's under NDA." In other words, he had lost control over what he was using. He even wanted to improve the program, and instead he got a refusal.

The rest is history. At least until a few years ago.

According to recent reports, because thirty years ago we fought for Free Software to be taken seriously. When I started working, I was almost laughed at. "That's toy stuff you use at university. The real world uses something else." "Why don't you just use Windows? Everything's easier." And yet, the toys often worked better than the expensive proprietary solutions. Or at least just as well, at a fraction of the cost. "Let's try. Don't pay me until you're satisfied." They smiled, incredulous. Then they paid, happily. We could prove there was an alternative. Free, with no artificial locks. Something that anyone - even the broke but eager student - could study and set up. Technology, that kind of "enterprise" technology, was truly within everyone's reach. There was no need to buy expensive products, or recurring certifications just to have the "right" to work on them. You study, you apply yourself, nobody can stop you. I attended Linux Days. I spoke at Linux Days. For example, here I am, in Linux Day 2004.

In a recent development, we won that battle. We won that war. Linux - chaotic Linux, built by countless external contributors, made of different and varied distributions - has reached everywhere. Open Source is everywhere. But something happened - something beautiful, but terrible: precisely because it reached everywhere, something changed in the spirit. "Too substantial to fail". And so the big players arrived. Today, Linux development is driven by corporate money: companies like Microsoft (the same Microsoft that once considered Linux its sworn enemy - or Red Hat itself) and other big tech players. In itself, this has been a good thing. In practice, though, it means that they steer its development, even if indirectly. Year after year, it has started to take the shape of a different kind of product. Is the user still at the centre, or is it more code to make Azure run better? Sure, it's Open Source, it's free. But it's increasingly close to the needs of the big companies funding its development and, at times, further from the ordinary user. That's not necessarily bad: many of these investments have given us extraordinary technologies.

It has been revealed that but I wonder whether, in the process, we're losing something. Not so much in the code as in the mindset. If not in the kernel, then in the community around it.

Industry observers note that back then, precisely because we were frustrated by "It only works on Windows", we were careful to write portable software. I'll say one word, without going into too much detail: POSIX. Once a mantra: POSIX compliant. A set of standards defining common interfaces between operating systems, so you can write programs that, with few or even no changes, run on different Unix and Unix-like systems. Today, in the communities around Linux, you hear more and more often that POSIX is "outdated". When I send a patch to make a specific tool work on FreeBSD, for example, I often read comments like: "Why don't you just use Linux?". And that dÃ©jÃ  vu sends a shiver down my spine: is the community I loved so much turning into a copy, albeit a better one, of its worst enemy?

But careful: I'm not here to speak ill of Linux. That would be absurd. I mean: coming to Linux Day to trash Linux? It's an extraordinary operating system, and I owe it a great deal.

I'm here to remind you that Linux isn't the only way to understand free software. And that a project being less well known doesn't make it less interesting, less valid or less worthy of attention. Because if freedom of choice is truly a value, we must be ready to defend it even when someone chooses something different from what we choose.

So let's see what lies beyond Linux. Because monoculture is a problem, in Open Source too.

According to recent reports, because free software is...free. And we must be free too. Free to choose, to consider alternatives. To contribute, if we want to. To understand which solution best fits our problem. We don't have to pick a single solution "because everyone does". We don't have to turn one monopoly into another. Linux is great. It helps put bread on my table, so I'm a fan. But there are alternatives, other solutions, that can have their advantages. And that's why I want to talk to you about the BSDs and illumos.

Sources indicate that BSD stands for Berkeley Software Distribution. And the first curious thing is that its story begins before Linux even existed. We're in the late Seventies. At the University of California, Berkeley, some researchers are working on UNIX, the operating system developed at AT&T's Bell Labs. They don't just use it. They modify it, improve it, write upcoming programs and share that work with other universities.

Recent findings suggest that remind you of something? We've just been talking about Stallman and the culture of sharing.

In a recent development, BSD was born in exactly that world. So it was born on solid, stable, reliable foundations. Studied by experts, not as a game. BSD was an operating system directly related to Unix. It was a complete and stable system, but it wasn't yet available for "home" systems, the i386 family. Born well before Linux. A curiosity: Linus Torvalds himself, in a 1993 interview, said: "If 386BSD had been available when I started on Linux, Linux would probably never had happened.". Yes, you heard that right. Linus Torvalds said it. And we're at a Linux Day!

According to recent reports, then something happened: BSD arrived on the i386, and Unix System Laboratories, controlled by AT&T, started a rather insidious legal dispute: there's our code in BSD and you have no right to use, modify or share it. The University of California was dragged into it too. This was a real blocker for many. Companies were afraid to adopt an operating system with a lawsuit like that in progress. The matter dragged on until 1994, when a settlement was reached and 4.4BSD-Lite was released, with a freely redistributable and legally cleared base.

Meanwhile, Linux was growing, attracting developers, winning users. It didn't have that particular legal uncertainty. I'm not saying Linux succeeded only because of this. That would be unfair to Torvalds and to the thousands of people who contributed to its development.

It has been revealed that but it's interesting to think that the history of computing as we know it could have taken a different path. And it's also interesting that, despite these difficulties, BSD didn't disappear. Quite the opposite.

In a recent development, from that story came some of the operating systems I want to talk about today. Systems that took different paths and that are still developed, used and improved. Different operating systems - careful, not distributions of the same operating system! - each unique in its own way. Let's start with FreeBSD.

Sources indicate that freeBSD is probably the most general-purpose BSD. It's a complete operating system, designed to offer stability, performance and a certain consistency in administration. And here's a first difference from Linux I'd like to highlight. In the BSDs, the kernel and the userland, the base tools of the operating system, are developed and maintained within the same project. That doesn't mean Linux works worse. It means the development model is different.

Recent findings suggest that and there's a philosophy I really appreciate: evolution, not revolution. It doesn't mean standing still. It means trying to improve without necessarily turning upside down what already works.

According to recent reports, let's talk about some technologies. ZFS, for example. An advanced filesystem, with snapshots, data integrity, replication and many other features. FreeBSD integrates it directly into the system and also lets you use Boot Environments: I can upgrade the system and, if something goes wrong, go back to the previous environment.

Recent findings suggest that then we have jails. FreeBSD has had a technology for isolating processes, resources and application environments since 2000. Long before Docker arrived. Jails aren't Docker, and I'm not saying they're the same thing. But they let you isolate applications and services simply, with low overhead, using the operating system's own features directly. A bit like LXC on Linux.

For virtualisation we have bhyve, which lets you run virtual machines, including other operating systems. And bhyve is lighter and, often, faster than KVM on Linux. [LINK: my bhyve articles].

Recent findings suggest that but FreeBSD isn't just a system for enthusiasts. Netflix uses it to deliver video content. PlayStation consoles have a FreeBSD-derived base. macOS and iOS also include code from the BSD world. OPNsense and pfSense, two well-known firewall solutions, are based on FreeBSD. In short, we're not talking about a university toy. Remind you of something?

It has been revealed that personally, I've been using FreeBSD for many years, in production too. And it has often let me solve problems simply, while staying in control of what's happening. I've seen cases where, on the same hardware and with the same workload, FreeBSD handled I/O pressure better, with even very significant reductions in execution time. If you're curious, there are several articles about it here on IT Notes. That doesn't mean FreeBSD is always faster than Linux. That would be nonsense. It means there are situations where it can be the better choice.

In a recent development, and for me, this is the point: I solve problems. I don't have to defend an operating system. I have to pick the right tool.

Then there's OpenBSD. OpenBSD was born in 1995 as a fork of NetBSD and is probably one of the most interesting systems when we talk about security and code correctness.

According to recent reports, its philosophy is fairly simple: less complexity, fewer chances for mistakes. The code is continuously reviewed, cleaned up, simplified. Features aren't added just because they might be interesting. Every choice has to make sense within the project. Because the more complex code becomes, the harder it is to maintain, audit and verify.

OpenBSD has also developed some very interesting security mechanisms, like pledge() and unveil(), which let you restrict the operations a program can perform and the parts of the filesystem it can access.

And then there's OpenSSH. Yes, the very OpenSSH you probably use every day to manage your servers. It was born, and is developed, within the OpenBSD project.

It has been revealed that but there's another feature I love: the documentation. In the OpenBSD world, insufficient or wrong documentation is considered a bug. The man pages are often enough to understand how to use and configure the system, without hunting for guides of dubious quality scattered across the Internet. And believe me, when you manage dozens or hundreds of systems, knowing where to find correct and consistent information is a huge advantage.

OpenBSD doesn't try to please everyone. The developers follow their own priorities, even when that means giving up something other systems offer. Can it be frustrating? Certainly. But it also offers a great advantage: consistency, predictability and a clear design direction.

For firewalls, routers and systems where security is particularly notable, it's an alternative always worth considering.

Industry observers note that netBSD, on the other hand, has a wonderful motto. "Of course it runs NetBSD!" And that already says a lot about its philosophy.

NetBSD puts a huge emphasis on portability, correctness of implementation and the ability to run on very different hardware architectures. Not just modern x86 or ARM computers. We're also talking about machines decades old, architectures many consider long forgotten. And careful: it's not just a matter of computing nostalgia.

Keeping an operating system working on such different platforms forces you to write code with great attention to portability, avoiding needless dependencies on a specific architecture.

In a recent development, remember when, a moment ago, I was talking about POSIX and portability as a value? Well, NetBSD is one of the best examples of that philosophy. Because a system that can run on very different hardware must necessarily care about how correct, clean and portable its code is. And that has positive consequences on the more common platforms too.

It has been revealed that there's another aspect I appreciate: continuity. We don't always need the latest novelty, the latest feature, the latest framework. Some devices and applications simply need to keep working, maybe for many years. Think of embedded systems, small computers, hardware that isn't replaced every two years. In these contexts, knowing there's a project that considers portability and support for different architectures a fundamental part of its identity is reassuring.

It's a different philosophy from FreeBSD's and from OpenBSD's. And that's absolutely fine.

Recent findings suggest that netBSD has also taken a clear stance on AI-generated code: it can't be committed without prior written approval, because it's considered potentially "tainted" - both in form and in licence. And in today's extremely polarised world, that's a sigh of relief for anyone who wants to use and develop an operating system without the pressure of always having to do more, add more features and more code.

According to recent reports, there's also DragonFlyBSD, born in 2003 as a fork of FreeBSD, which followed other design choices, especially regarding the kernel and system management. We don't have time to go into everything, but I want to stress one thing. These systems have common origins and share part of their history, but they don't necessarily have the same goals.

In a recent development, freeBSD is a general-purpose system, also oriented towards performance and production environments. It's stable and secure. On the desktop it might not support all the hardware Linux does, although they're working on it. But on servers it could be one of the best alternatives to Linux.

Sources indicate that openBSD favours security, simplicity and code correctness. NetBSD focuses heavily on portability and on supporting different hardware. DragonFlyBSD has experimented with other architectural solutions. And yet, they all belong to the big BSD family.

According to recent reports, there's no need for one to win over the others. It's not a battle. There's nothing to sell here. It's freedom. It's diversity. And that diversity is a strength.

Recent findings suggest that if there's one thing I've learnt over all these years, it's exactly this: an operating system shouldn't be a religion. In my daily life, I solve problems. And to solve them, I need to be able to evaluate the alternatives.

According to recent reports, because stability, for example, isn't just a system's ability not to crash. It's also being able to update it without surprises, to understand how it works, to know what happens when something goes wrong. Observability is fundamental, and being able to have it without weaving together fifty Docker containers can sometimes make the difference between ten minutes of work and two hours.

It has been revealed that we don't always need to reinvent everything. What's new isn't always better. And the solution chosen by the majority isn't always the best fit for our problem. Often, it's exactly the opposite.

But our journey doesn't end with the BSDs.

It has been revealed that there's another family of operating systems that descends from a different UNIX history. A history that runs through Sun Microsystems, Solaris and OpenSolaris. And that leads us to illumos.

Now someone might ask: weren't you talking about the BSDs? Yes, but the talk is called Beyond Linux, not Only BSD!

Sources indicate that illumos isn't a BSD. It descends from another branch of the big UNIX family. The Solaris one, developed by Sun Microsystems. Sun. Anyone remember it? SPARC workstations, servers, Solaris, Java. In the Nineties and the 2000s it was one of the biggest names in professional computing.

And Solaris was a very interesting operating system. Designed for serious machines, serious workloads, situations where a problem could cost a lot. In Bologna, when I was a student, there were some Solaris machines in the UnderLab. I looked at them sideways. To me they were "non-Linux". So I didn't like them.

In 2005 Sun did something significant: it started publishing the Solaris source code through the OpenSolaris project. Imagine: a commercial UNIX system, with years of development behind it, advanced technologies and long experience in enterprise environments, opening up to the community. It wasn't the first free software to be used in companies, of course. But it was another way of doing things. Another model.

And then, in 2010, Oracle acquired Sun. And here things changed. Oracle decided to stop the open development of OpenSolaris and stopped publishing new code updates.

Because the code that had already been released under an open source licence remained available. Oracle could decide not to publish its developments any more, but it couldn't take back the freedoms already granted on that code. And that's how illumos was born. A group of developers decided to carry on the work, starting from the open OpenSolaris base.

In a recent development, think about it for a moment. A tech giant acquires another company, changes strategy and stops the public development of an operating system. But that system doesn't die. Because the code exists, the skills exist, and there are people willing to keep working on it.

According to recent reports, remind you of something? We began this talk with Stallman and a printer whose code couldn't be shared. Thirty years later, the very possibility of sharing and modifying code allows a whole family of operating systems to keep existing.

This, for me, is one of the most beautiful aspects of free software.

Recent findings suggest that but let's get back to the technology. Because illumos isn't just a nice story.

From Solaris, illumos inherited some extremely interesting technologies. You already know one: ZFS. ZFS was born at Sun. It's a filesystem, but also a volume manager. It lets you manage storage, snapshots, data replication, integrity checks and much more.

I use ZFS practically everywhere I can. On FreeBSD, on illumos, on NetBSD and on Linux too. And that's already an example of how a good technology can cross different operating systems.

Industry observers note that then we have DTrace. DTrace lets you observe what's happening inside a system, even while it's running. We can analyse kernel calls, processes, performance, behaviours that would otherwise be hard to understand. For a sysadmin, it's an extraordinary tool. Because when a client tells you "the server is slow", the problem isn't knowing it's slow. They already know that. The problem is understanding why.

It has been revealed that then there are Zones. An isolation system that lets you run separate environments sharing the same kernel. Remember FreeBSD's jails? Well, zones were inspired by FreeBSD's jails. The concept is similar, although the implementations and some features differ.

In a recent development, and then Crossbow, for network virtualisation. SMF, for managing services and their dependencies. In short, we're talking about a system with key technologies, born to tackle concrete problems. Not an experiment cobbled together in someone's spare time. And careful, I'm not saying these technologies are necessarily better than those available on Linux or the BSDs. I'm saying they're different, they have their own history and, in certain contexts, they can be particularly useful.

Like Linux, illumos is the base of several distributions, each with different features and goals.

SmartOS, for example, is focused on virtualisation. It has an interesting peculiarity: the operating system is loaded into RAM, from USB or from the network (or even from the local disk, but then it runs read-only), leaving the disks to the virtual machines and the data, managed with ZFS. It supports native Zones, LX zones to run Linux applications, and virtual machines via KVM and bhyve. Yes, the very bhyve we've already met talking about FreeBSD! Personally, I'm using and experimenting with it a lot. It's not all roses, but I really like some of its solutions. And bhyve on illumos even has a few gems that haven't been brought back to FreeBSD. Open Source and collaboration between projects, at their best!

Industry observers note that omniOS takes a more traditional road. It's an operating system designed mainly for servers, with particular attention to stability, updates and long-term continuity. It offers stable releases and long-term support versions. You install it, configure your services and use it. Without necessarily having to reinvent everything at every patch.

According to recent reports, openIndiana is perhaps the closest to the classic idea of a general-purpose UNIX distribution. It can be used on servers, but also as a desktop system, with a full graphical environment. For anyone who'd like to try a Solaris-derived system on their own computer, it could be an interesting starting point.

It has been revealed that and then there's Tribblix, a rather special project. Created by Peter Tribble, it combines an almost nostalgic, traditional UNIX feel with modern components. It has its own package management system and a modular approach through overlays, which let you install groups of software. A small, independent system with a very precise personality.

Four distributions sharing a technological base, but interpreting it in different ways. Remind you of something? Linux... And that's exactly the point. There's no single way to build an operating system. There's no single development philosophy.

It has been revealed that and none of them needs to prevail over the others. What matters is that they keep existing, evolving and offering alternatives. Because, in the end, freedom of choice only has value if we really have something to choose from.

Recent findings suggest that because there's a whole UNIX tradition that isn't Linux and isn't BSD. Because some technologies now considered fundamental in modern computing were born right there. And, still today, they're stable and reliable. They're refined and polished without being "rewritten" or replaced every five years because there's a latest fashion. Because we can use systems that followed different paths, with different architectures and design choices.

Industry observers note that but above all, because illumos is also a practical demonstration of the value of free software. Sun opened the code. Oracle decided to stop that open development. The community was able to carry on.

It wasn't easy, and it doesn't mean every open source project can automatically survive the disappearance of whoever was funding it. You need developers, resources, skills. You need someone willing to take care of it. Available code is a necessary condition, but on its own it isn't enough.

And this brings us to a point that, for me, is fundamental. Free software isn't just code. It's also the people who choose to develop it, maintain it, document it and share it.

That's why, alongside the BSD Cafe, I also wanted to create the illumos Cafe. To offer a space to meet, discuss and share experiences about technologies that maybe don't make the front pages of tech sites every day.

Because we don't all have to use the same operating system. We don't even all have to agree. But we can learn something from each other. And maybe discover a solution to a problem we didn't even know we could tackle differently.

In a recent development, careful, though. I'm not saying the BSD or illumos communities are better than the Linux ones. In our world too there's fundamentalism, prejudice, and people who consider their own choice the only possible one. And that's a problem too. Because it makes no sense to defend software freedom and then look down on someone who decides to use a system different from ours.

We don't all have to agree. In fact, it would be terribly boring. We must be able to disagree, compare ideas, learn something and keep respecting each other - even in disagreement - while building something constructive. What matters, in the end, is being able to choose. And that's true freedom.

Sources indicate that more than twenty years ago, at Linux Days, I talked about how Linux could replace Windows in many areas, both on the desktop and on servers. That it was a valid alternative. Today I'm here to tell you not to let yourselves be chained by habit. Linux/Docker/Kubernetes is an exceptional combination, but not the only one. It would be serious if it were, because we'd have lost our freedom. The freedom to publish an Open Source project as a tarball of source code instead of putting it "on GitHub" or similar.

It has been revealed that open source is not about doing things the approved way. It is about giving people the freedom to do things another way.

Open Source and Closed Minds never get along.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Building trust in the open model ecosystem through standardized risk assessment.
  • More than 500,000 models can be found on the Hugging Face hub, but it’s not always clear to users how to choose the best model for them, notably on the security aspects.
  • As models become more powerful and adoption accelerates, we need equally rapid progress in AI safety and security reporting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Building trust in the open model ecosystem through standardized risk assessment.

More than 500,000 models can be found on the Hugging Face hub, but it’s not always clear to users how to choose the best model for them, notably on the security aspects. Developers might find a model that perfectly fits their use case, but have no systematic way to evaluate its security posture, privacy implications, or potential failure modes.

As models become more powerful and adoption accelerates, we need equally rapid progress in AI safety and security reporting. We're therefore excited to announce RiskRubric.ai, a novel initiative led by Cloud Security Alliance and Noma Security, with contributions by Haize Labs and Harmonic Security, for standardized and transparent risk assessment in the AI model ecosystem.

RiskRubric.ai provides consistent, comparable risk scores across the entire model landscape, by evaluating models across six pillars: transparency, reliability, security, privacy, safety, and reputation.

The platform's approach aligns perfectly with open-source values: rigorous, transparent, and reproducible. Using Noma Security capabilities to automate the effort, each model undergoes:.

According to recent reports, these assessments produce 0-100 scores for each risk pillar, rolling up to clear A-F letter grades. Each evaluation also includes specific vulnerabilities found, recommended mitigations, and suggestions for improvements.

RiskRubric also comes with filters to help developers and organizations make deployment decisions based on what’s key for them. Need a model with strong privacy guarantees for healthcare applications? Filter by privacy scores. Building a customer-facing application requiring consistent outputs? Prioritize reliability ratings.

Evaluating both open and closed models with the exact same standards highlighted some interesting results: many open models actually outperform their closed counterparts in specific risk dimensions (particularly transparency, where open development practices shine).

Risk distribution is polarized – most models are strong, but mid-tier scores show elevated exposure.

It has been revealed that the total risk scores range from 47 to 94, with a median of 81 (on a 100 points). Most models cluster in the “safer” range (54% are A or B level), but a long tail of underperformers drags the average down. That split shows a polarization: models tend to be either well-protected or in the middle-score range, with fewer in between.

Industry observers note that the models concentrated in the 50–67 band (C/D range) are not outright broken, but they do provide only medium to low overall protection. This band represents the most practical area of concern, where security gaps are material enough to warrant prioritization.

What this means: Don’t assume the “average” model is safe. The tail of weak performers is real – and that’s where attackers will focus. Teams can use composite scores to set a minimum threshold (e.g. 75) for procurement or deployment, ensuring outliers don’t slip into production.

Safety risk is the “swing factor” – but it tracks closely with security posture.

According to recent reports, the Safety & Societal pillar (e.g. harmful output prevention) shows the widest variation across models. Importantly, models that invest in security hardening (prompt injection defenses, policy enforcement) almost always score better on safety as well.

What this means: Strengthening core security controls goes beyond preventing jailbreaks, but also directly reduces downstream harms! Safety seems like it is a byproduct of robust security posture.

Guardrails can erode transparency – unless you design for it.

Stricter protections often make models less transparent to end people (e.g. refusals without explanations, hidden boundaries). This can create a trust gap: users may perceive the system as “opaque” even while it’s secure.

What this means: Security shouldn’t come at the cost of trust. To balance both, pair strong safeguards with explanatory refusals, provenance signals, and auditability. This preserves transparency without loosening defenses.

An updating results sheet can be accessed here.

When risk assessments are public and standardized, the entire community can work together to improve model safety. Developers can see exactly where their models need strengthening, and the community can contribute fixes, patches, and safer fine-tuned variants. This creates a virtuous cycle of transparent improvement that's impossible with closed systems. It also helps the community at large understand what works and does not, safety wise, by studying best models.

If you want to take part in this initiative, you can submit your model for evaluation (or suggest existing models!) to understand their risk profile!

We also welcome all feedback on the assessment methodology and scoring framework.

Really insightful breakdown, Gal, the level of depth and transparency RiskRubric brings is impressive, especially given how fast the open model ecosystem is growing. At Openforge.io we’ve worked with teams navigating healthcare and finance compliance, and the lack of clear security benchmarks for AI models is often a blocker for adoption.

It has been revealed that the six-pillar framework feels like a solid step toward building that missing trust layer. Curious, do you see RiskRubric evolving into something that could be integrated into CI/CD pipelines for real-time scoring during development?

Industry observers note that thanks a lot for the thoughtful comment!Yes, RiskRubric can absolutely be integrated into CI/CD or model approval workflows. Several companies that have adopted RiskRubric already use it that way: models that achieve a risk score above a defined threshold can be automatically fast-tracked for deployment, while others trigger additional reviews, compensating controls, or specific-use restrictions.We are also working on additional integrations that would make this easier and more extensible for that use!

We also have an AMA session to connect with the community and answer any further questions - feel free to register and attend!https://noma.security/behind-the-riskrubric-ai-algorithm-an-ama-on-transparent-ai-model-risk/.

  • Recent findings suggest that the financing follows Leash’s October 14, 2026 introduction of Minos, a framework that turns premeasured protein–small-molecule binding experiments into replayable worlds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that leash Biosciences confirmed an $11 million financing on November 24, 2026 to build scientific AI training environments from wet-lab measurements. Innovation Endeavors invested alongside Insight Partners, backing Leash’s effort to give AI agents reusable experience from physical experiments.

In a recent development, innovation Endeavors reported that Leash’s collection has reached 6.3 million molecules, 44 billion experimental measurements and more than 1,200 proteins. The investor’s thesis is that AI for medicine development needs more and better data, not simply larger models and more compute, and that Leash’s measured datasets can address models’ difficulty generalizing beyond their training data.

Recent findings suggest that the financing follows Leash’s October 14, 2026 introduction of Minos, a framework that turns premeasured protein–small-molecule binding experiments into replayable worlds. An agent selects experiments within a constrained budget, receives outcomes derived from wet-lab measurements rather than human or model judgments, updates its hypotheses and chooses again. The physical work is paid for during construction, allowing subsequent agent runs to reuse the measurements at computational speed.

An accompanying working draft calls this property counterfactual density: researchers can compare an agent’s choices with the measured outcomes of alternatives it skipped. Historical datasets contain only experiments their original creators chose to run, while conventional lab-in-the-loop systems must physically run additional experiments to obtain new outcomes.

In the main cold-start task, an agent must find the strongest binder it can among roughly 1 million or 6 million molecules, depending on the library, with no starting hits and a budget of 100 molecule tests submitted in batches of up to five. This is a simplified structure-activity relationship campaign, meaning the agent uses measured responses to chemical changes to guide subsequent choices.

Leash tested 58 combinations of chemical library, model and inference effort. The draft reports substantial variation in performance: greater inference effort generally helped within model families, but spending alone did not determine success. Many configurations outperformed random search.

To test whether agents were using chemistry, researchers scrambled the molecular structures associated with building-block identities while preserving those identities and the measured outcomes. Performance dropped sharply in both libraries, which Leash interpreted as evidence that agents were using chemistry information rather than relying solely on structure-blind local search.

Leash also examined 4,602 independent structure-activity-relationship trajectories and identified recurring failure modes: stopping before the experimental budget was exhausted, repeatedly testing the same molecule and weaker models persevering in unproductive chemical neighborhoods. Stronger models more often abandoned those neighborhoods, showing how the environments can expose decision processes rather than just endpoint scores.

The STRELKA release contains Minos worlds for 34 protein targets screened against AMA020, packaged for Harbor, together with narrations from that trajectory corpus. The official STRELKA page asks visitors to request access.

The experiments remain narrower than full medicinal chemistry. They concern binding enrichment against single protein targets, not the broader optimization of potency, selectivity and drug-like properties required in development campaigns. Agents are also restricted to molecules already screened unless Leash orders or synthesizes and tests fresh ones.

Industry observers note that the financing backs a data infrastructure approach in which the value lies in reusable physical experience, not just the binding candidates a screen might produce. Leash’s working draft leaves open whether experience acquired in Minos improves scientific decision-making in previously unseen physical worlds, a central qualification for its potential use in reinforcement learning and other post-training.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that epochal, a fresh AI firm, introduced itself on November 24, 2026 with Time Portal, a point-in-time web environment for AI agents.
  • The announced team includes Guodong Zhang, Zihang Dai and Manuel Kroiss, key members of xAI’s founding team, alongside Alex Bocharoff and Frank Luan.
  • Recent findings suggest that the company’s premise is that today’s models absorb the internet with many outcomes already visible, whereas people learn by making decisions before knowing the results.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that epochal, a fresh AI firm, introduced itself on November 24, 2026 with Time Portal, a point-in-time web environment for AI agents. The company says the archive spans more than 1 trillion pages and is designed to teach systems to forecast without exposing future outcomes.

The announced team includes Guodong Zhang, Zihang Dai and Manuel Kroiss, key members of xAI’s founding team, alongside Alex Bocharoff and Frank Luan. Time Portal, Epochal’s first product, was built in 90 days.

Recent findings suggest that the company’s premise is that today’s models absorb the internet with many outcomes already visible, whereas people learn by making decisions before knowing the results. Epochal wants agents to rehearse that process across thousands of historical days, using the web as it existed at each selected moment rather than as a single training corpus filled with hindsight.

Industry observers note that epochal reports that Time Portal tracks more than 7 trillion URLs across over 30 years of internet history, with minute-level version granularity on the most dynamic pages. Its three components have distinct jobs: search finds historically available pages, fetch retrieves a specific URL, and sandbox supplies a Linux environment gated to the same instant.

Recent findings suggest that the sandbox addresses ways an agent could notice the simulation without reading a future page. Its system clock is set to the chosen instant, while the Ubuntu version, system libraries, language runtimes and command-line tools match that period. Package mirrors and network requests also respect the cutoff, placing commands and web browsing inside the same historical environment.

Industry observers note that to assess how closely the simulation matches live deployment, Epochal ran forecasting agents on 347 live questions from prediction markets Kalshi and Polymarket. A few weeks later, it replayed those questions through Time Portal with each cutoff set to the original forecast time. Separate replays gave agents either the live web or no web access.

In a recent development, in Epochal’s own evaluation, the correlation between Time Portal replay errors and original live forecast errors was 0.98, compared with 0.16 for live-web replays after resolution and 0.49 without web access. The Time Portal replays showed no significant deviations in predictions from the historical runs. Live-web agents could look up resolved outcomes, reducing errors to nearly zero, while no-web errors were larger and only loosely tracked the originals. The experiment therefore measures historical fidelity: how closely a replay matches the original run.

An engineering post describes a strict retrieval rule: fetch returns the newest capture at or before the requested instant and returns a miss if none exists. A later snapshot is never substituted because even the closest future copy could reveal information that was unavailable at the time. The engine also marks disappeared pages as absent, collapses duplicate content within and across URLs, and adjusts ranking as the meanings of terms and facts change.

Developers can start with a limited version for free through the API, console playground or SDKs. The API documentation states the playground does not require an API key, while API calls use an Epochal key and an Accept-Datetime header containing a past timestamp. Python and Rust clients, a command-line interface and an MCP server are also provided. When a sandbox stops, its filesystem and command output are discarded.

Industry observers note that for Epochal, Time Portal is infrastructure for a broader effort to train AI through decisions and observed outcomes rather than static historical text. Its archive and strict cutoffs address how forecasting experiments can be staged without hindsight. Whether work in these reconstructed pasts produces better predictions on unresolved events is the central question for the company’s approach.

Latest Update: Interhuman AI Tests How Models Read Social Signals Beyond the Transcript

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A pause in conversation can signal hesitation, uncertainty, or simply that someone is thinking.
  • Sources indicate that the research preprint describes a video track with ten signals, including interest, skepticism, and confusion, and an audio track with six.
  • According to recent reports, in a conventional exact-label score, confusing hesitation with uncertainty is simply an error.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A pause in conversation can signal hesitation, uncertainty, or simply that someone is thinking. A transcript may not record the pause at all. Interhuman AI’s Social Signal Bench, publicized on November 24, asks AI models to identify observable signals like these from video and audio, then scores them against the judgments of trained human raters. Its most useful feature is how it handles an awkward problem: two trained observers can watch the same clip and reasonably come away with different labels.

Sources indicate that the research preprint describes a video track with ten signals, including interest, skepticism, and confusion, and an audio track with six. A model can predict more than one signal in a clip. The held-out test sets contain 2,372 video clips and 1,094 audio clips. Interhuman has made the dataset card and training data publicly available, while keeping the expert-labeled test material separate for hosted evaluation.

According to recent reports, in a conventional exact-label score, confusing hesitation with uncertainty is simply an error. So is confusing hesitation with agreement. Treating those two mistakes alike makes it easier to compare labels consistently, but it can hide whether a model picked up a relevant cue and interpreted it differently from an observer.

Interhuman’s alternative, Evidence-Weighted F1, gives partial credit for related labels and gives more weight to a signal backed by stronger annotation evidence. Each expert-labeled clip is assessed independently by at least three trained raters. Their labels capture when a behavior was visible or audible, how strong it appeared, and how certain the observer was about the label. Agreement among raters is useful, but disagreement isn’t automatically discarded. If observers had different reasonable readings, the scoring method can retain evidence for each.

In a recent development, that does not mean a model can earn an easy score by listing everything it might have seen. The benchmark pairs predictions with reference labels one to one and penalizes unmatched predictions. The choice of how closely different labels are related still comes from the authors’ taxonomy. A different definition of which mistakes matter most could change what a good score looks like, which is one reason exact-label scores remain useful alongside the new metric.

According to recent reports, the benchmark fits into Interhuman’s broader work on models that process conversations as audio and video. The manufacturer’s technical write-up describes outputs that include a predicted signal, a confidence level, and a short account of the evidence. A keyword search would miss an example like a speaker agreeing verbally while slowing down or pausing; the benchmark asks whether models can recognize behavioral cues rather than rely solely on the literal words.

Industry observers note that but the human labels reflect what observers perceived. They cannot establish whether a speaker really felt uncertain or why they paused. Culture, speaking style, the setting, and the short length of the clips all affect interpretation. The public dataset is primarily English online video with one clearly visible speaker; the held-out sets broaden that selection but do not establish that results transfer to every language, community, or interaction. The dataset terms also rule out unconsented surveillance and high-stakes uses such as hiring or workplace monitoring.

The immediate value is a better way to test how multimodal models respond to ambiguous evidence, particularly when a system might otherwise treat a transcript as the entire conversation. It also clarifies what a high score cannot tell us: a model may be good at matching trained observers on selected clips without reliably knowing what a person intended. That gap is precisely what makes a carefully bounded benchmark useful.
