📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, deepHealth declared on November 24, 2026 that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration had cleared Mammo Risk through the 510(k) pathway. The software estimates three-, four- and five-year breast cancer risk from an existing 3D mammogram and is commercially available to healthcare providers across the United States.

The clearance is dated November 23, 2026. DeepHealth describes Mammo Risk as the first FDA-cleared image-based breast-cancer risk-prediction solution for 3D mammography, including combined 3D/2D imaging workflows. Its intended role is to flag patients with no apparent signs of cancer whose mammograms nevertheless suggest elevated future risk, giving clinicians information for personalized screening pathways and consideration of supplemental imaging. The output concerns future risk rather than detection of an existing tumor, and no additional scan is required.

Victoria Smart, senior vice president of mission at Susan G. Komen, noted: “Everyone’s biology and breast cancer risk are different, yet too often we take a one-size-fits-all approach to screening and care.”.

It has been revealed that deepHealth says the AI was trained on 220,000 studies and derives personalized risk estimates directly from routine mammogram images, unlike conventional assessment approaches that rely on extensive patient questionnaires and clinical information. The software is compatible with supported systems from multiple vendors.

DeepHealth reports that an independent, multicenter pivotal study of more than 65,000 screening mammograms at 10 U.S. clinical sites demonstrated strong predictive performance, with consistent results across subgroups including Black women and women with dense breasts.

It has been revealed that mammo Risk builds on earlier DeepHealth technology designed to predict risk up to two years ahead. That technology was CE-marked and commercially available in Europe, with clinical validation across European and U.S. screening populations using both 2D and 3D mammography. The cleared version extends the prediction horizon to three, four and five years.

Industry observers note that the 2022 study in Science Translational Medicine, led by Karolinska Institutet researchers, documents the earlier model. It used a nested case-control design drawn from 154,200 multiethnic women aged 35 to 74 who underwent digital breast tomosynthesis, or 3D mammography, screening in the United States between 2014 and 2019. The analysis included 805 incident cancers and 5,173 matched healthy women.

The paper reports that the model was developed to predict late-stage and interval cancers after negative screening exams. Its one-year discrimination, a measure of how well it distinguished women who developed cancer from those who did not, was 0.82, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.79 to 0.85. Under the high-risk threshold used in the paper, 14% of women met the cutoff; that group contained 76% of stage II and III cancers and 59% of stage 0 cancers.

Sources indicate that those results concern the earlier research model, not Mammo Risk’s pivotal study. The paper also discloses iCAD funding and an image-based risk-patent license to iCAD.

Mammo Risk joins DeepHealth’s Radiology AI Suite and complements Mammo Dx, pairing future-risk prediction with cancer-detection technology. DeepHealth, a wholly owned subsidiary of RadNet, intends to integrate Mammo Risk into RadNet’s mammography screening initiatives, including the Enhanced Breast Cancer Detection program. The integration is planned rather than completed.

The American Medical Association’s CPT Category III code descriptors list 1137T and 1138T for algorithm-derived five-year breast malignancy risk scores with automated results. Code 1137T applies to a screening-mammogram dataset acquired in a separate session, while 1138T applies to a dataset acquired in the same session. Both were released to the AMA website on October 2, 2026, and take effect January 1, 2027.

The AMA explains that Category III codes are temporary tools for collecting utilization and outcomes data on emerging services. Inclusion does not establish clinical efficacy, payer coverage or reimbursement, and payments depend on payer policies rather than a yearly fee schedule.

The clearance puts a future-risk tool into the U.S. market, while the AMA’s coding framework separates tracking from payment. The central practical question is whether the scores become part of screening decisions and whether the resulting utilization and outcomes evidence supports reimbursement by payers.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that fluidstack announced the launch of Blackbird on November 24, 2026, a modular data center platform designed for construction within six months of groundbreaking, alongside factory-built Compute Modules and Electrical Skids.
  • Factory fabrication is central to that schedule.
  • Fluidstack also expects the shorter schedule to bring tax revenue and permanent jobs to host communities 12 to 18 months sooner while minimizing local disruption from construction.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that fluidstack announced the launch of Blackbird on November 24, 2026, a modular data center platform designed for construction within six months of groundbreaking, alongside factory-built Compute Modules and Electrical Skids. The Blackbird design scales from a single 10 MW-plus zone to a 400 MW facility.

Factory fabrication is central to that schedule. Fluidstack compares the six-month design target with an industry standard of 18 to 24 months and expects remote fabrication and on-site modular assembly to reduce build time by two-thirds or more. The modules are designed to reach data center campuses as integrated and tested units before on-site assembly.

Fluidstack also expects the shorter schedule to bring tax revenue and permanent jobs to host communities 12 to 18 months sooner while minimizing local disruption from construction. Those community effects are projections attached to the accelerated build schedule.

It has been revealed that fluidstack’s Blackbird documentation describes an example compute zone with twelve Compute Modules arranged in four rows of three. Conveyance modules at both ends carry shared busway feeders, hydronic mains, and cable trays. Each row provides up to 120 linear feet of rack space, while the design accommodates any AI chip type, direct-to-chip liquid cooling, and rear rack fan coils.

Two example power configurations illustrate the trade-off between capacity and redundancy. Fluidstack lists approximately 14 MW per zone with N redundancy and a 95% availability target, or 10.5 MW with 4-makes-3 redundancy and a 99.9% availability target. Both configurations can operate at 415 V or 480 V.

Sources indicate that the Compute Module is the repeatable unit inside that layout. It is a self-supporting steel structure that carries power, cooling, and cabling above standard racks, with hot-aisle containment built in. Fluidstack specifies up to 4 MW of row capacity depending on configuration, a length of up to 53 feet, and compatibility with racks up to 60 inches deep. The module can be installed at an existing facility or integrated into Blackbird, and it is sized for transport on a standard flatbed.

The Electrical Skid handles the power-conversion path feeding those rows. Medium-voltage switching, a 3.6 MVA liquid-filled transformer, and low-voltage distribution sit on one skid. Its standard incoming supply is 35 kV class, with a tap changer selecting 480 V or 415 V output, and the enclosure is rated for outdoor use. Its factory acceptance initiative covers all Level 3 tests and part of Level 4; paired with Blackbird, the skid is designed to connect on site to factory-terminated low-voltage cables.

All three products will be manufactured at Fluidstack’s new Glendale, Arizona, plant, which spans more than 1.1 million square feet and uses globally sourced components. The manufacturer says the facility will support 1,250 permanent manufacturing and skilled-trades jobs.

Industry observers note that chief executive Gary Wu remarked the strategy is intended to bring industrial capacity back to the United States for components that foreign supply chains cannot deliver promptly enough. He described US engineering and design followed by assembly at construction sites across the country as a way to accelerate domestic AI infrastructure construction.

The factory plan also includes detailed module-production targets. With all parts on hand, Fluidstack targets three days to assemble a Compute Module, two days to test it, and one day to load it, with output of up to 32 modules per day, seven days per week. Compute Modules are planned to undergo Level 3 testing before shipment. Their UL listing remains pending, leaving a qualification step alongside the production and deployment targets.

The six-month proposition therefore depends on more than building modules quickly: it requires Fluidstack to sustain its stated factory output, complete the Compute Module’s UL listing, and reproduce the design’s availability and deployment targets at customer sites. That makes the Arizona plant’s production and subsequent site builds the measurable tests of whether modular construction can materially shorten the path to new AI capacity.

Accelerating Qwen3-8B Agent on Intel® Core™ Ultra with Depth-Pruned Draft Models

📅 29 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (818 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Qwen3-8B is one of the most exciting recent releases—a model with native agentic capabilities, making it a natural fit for the AIPC.
  • With OpenVINO.GenAI, we’ve been able to accelerate generation by ~1.3× using speculative decoding with a lightweight Qwen3-0.6B draft.
  • By using speculative decoding and applying a simple pruning process to the draft, we pushed the speedup even further to ~1.4×.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Qwen3-8B is one of the most exciting recent releases—a model with native agentic capabilities, making it a natural fit for the AIPC.

With OpenVINO.GenAI, we’ve been able to accelerate generation by ~1.3× using speculative decoding with a lightweight Qwen3-0.6B draft.

By using speculative decoding and applying a simple pruning process to the draft, we pushed the speedup even further to ~1.4×.

We wrapped this up by showing how these improvements can be used to run a fast, local AI Agent with 🤗 smolagents.

Qwen3-8B is part of the latest Qwen family, trained with explicit agentic behaviors. It supports tool invocation, multi-step reasoning, and long-context handling capabilities, that make it well-suited for complex agent workflows. When integrated with frameworks like Hugging Face 🤗smolagents, QwenAgent, or AutoGen, it enables a wide range of agentic applications built around tool use and reasoning. Unlike single-turn chatbots, agentic applications rely on reasoning models that produce “thinking aloud” traces, intermediate steps that expand token usage, making inference speed critical to responsiveness. The combination of optimized inference and built-in agentic intelligence makes Qwen3-8B a compelling foundation for next-gen AI agents.

We started by benchmarking the 4-bit optimized OpenVINO version of Qwen3-8B on an Intel Lunar Lake integrated GPU, establishing this as our baseline for further acceleration.

In a recent development, speculative decoding is a method to speed up auto-regressive generation. It works by using a smaller, faster model as a draft to propose multiple tokens in a single forward pass, which are then validated by the larger target model in one forward pass. In our setup, Qwen3-8B served as the target model while Qwen3-0.6B was used as the draft. This approach delivered an average of 1.3× speedup over the baseline.

Before initializing the LLMPipeline, make sure both the target and draft models are converted to OpenVINO. You can either download pre-converted models from the provided links or follow these instructions to convert your own.

According to recent reports, the speculative decoding speedup depends on the average number of generated tokens per forward step of the target, γ \gamma γ, the speculation window size, and the ratio between the target and draft models' latency c c c. A smaller, faster (though less accurate) draft can often deliver greater acceleration. This inspired us to shrink the draft model while still preserving its quality, i.e. E(#generated_tokens) E(\# generated\_tokens) E(#generated_tokens).

Speedup=E(#generated_tokens)γc+1 Speedup = \frac{E(\# generated\_tokens)}{\gamma c + 1} Speedup=γc+1E(#generated_tokens)​.

Our recent work shows that model depth (number of layers) is a major contributor to inference latency. We drew inspiration from recent work on layer-wise compression[1]. In our approach, we identify blocks of layers that contribute little, measured using angular distance, and remove them. After pruning, we apply fine-tuning to recover accuracy. Using this method, we pruned 6 out of 28 layers from the Qwen3-0.6B draft model. To recover the quality of the pruned draft model, we further finetuned it using synthetic data generated by Qwen3-8B. The data was produced by generating responses to 500k prompts from BAAI/Infinity-Instruct dataset.

Recent findings suggest that the resulting pruned draft model delivered ~1.4x speedup compared to the baseline, an improvement over the ~1.3× gain achieved with the original draft. This outcome aligns with theoretical expectations - reducing draft latency improves the over-all speedup, enabling faster and more efficient inference.

This demonstrates how pruning + speculative decoding can unlock faster and more efficient inference—making local AI agents even more practical.

Check out the notebook and the Qwen3-0.6B depth-pruned draft model to reproduce our results step by step.

According to recent reports, to showcase the real-world potential, we deployed our optimized setup with the 🤗smolagents library. With this integration, developers can plug in Qwen3-8B (paired with our pruned draft) to build agents that call APIs and external tools, write and execute code, handle long-context reasoning and run efficiently on Intel® Core™ Ultra. The benefits aren’t limited to Hugging Face, this model pairing can also be used seamlessly with frameworks like AutoGen or QwenAgent, further strengthening the agentic ecosystem.

In our demo, we assigned the accelerated Qwen3-based agent a task: 👉 Summarize the key features of the Qwen3 model series and present them in a slide deck.

Here’s how it worked: 1. The agent used a web search tool to gather up-to-date information. 2. It then switched to the Python interpreter to generate slides with the python-pptx library. This simple workflow highlights just a fraction of the possibilities unlocked when accelerated Qwen3 models meet frameworks like 🤗smolagents, bringing practical, efficient AI agents to life on AI PC. Try it here 🚀.

OpenAI Reports GPT-6 Designs Proteins With Reasoning and Code

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, openAI reported on November 24, 2026 that its GPT-6 family can design protein structures and amino-acid sequences using reasoning and general-purpose coding tools. In laboratory work with research partner Onava, some proteins based on GPT-6.2’s designs showed evidence of binding across five targets.

The research examines whether one general model can handle work usually divided among specialized protein systems. Those systems accept particular inputs and constraints, so fresh requirements can demand software changes or additional training. OpenAI’s approach instead uses natural-language instructions to specify details such as where a small protein called a minibinder should attach, its structural class, and the number of helices or strands it should contain.

Recent findings suggest that in the first laboratory experiment, a pre-release version of GPT-6.2 received three-dimensional structures of target proteins with the desired attachment sites marked. It wrote code to generate candidate minibinder shapes without specialized protein models. SolubleMPNN then proposed amino-acid sequences for those shapes, and other specialized systems helped select candidates predicted to fold correctly and bind at the intended site before Onava made and tested them.

OpenAI’s laboratory results show evidence of binding for 35 of 322 tested minibinders, or 10.9%, with at least one hit for each target. The same account cautions that earlier RFdiffusion experiments produced higher hit rates and that comparisons depend heavily on how strictly candidates are filtered and how binding is defined.

It has been revealed that A separate experiment withheld original amino-acid sequences and asked GPT-6.2 to redesign them from three-dimensional minibinder structures. For three unpublished structures that GPT-6.2 had itself generated, 14 of 107 proteins made from its upcoming sequences, or 13.1%, showed binding. OpenAI presents the unpublished starting structures and substantial sequence differences as strong evidence that the capability extends beyond memorization.

The antibody experiments focused on redesigning the loops that help an antibody attach to its target. OpenAI reports that 128 of 182 loop designs, or 70%, across six small VHH antibodies targeting IL-4Rα showed signs of binding. Separately, 179 of 272 fragments derived from five therapeutic antibodies, or 66%, showed binding to their original PD-1 or PD-L1 targets after roughly half the amino acids in each of three binding loops were changed.

OpenAI says an internal research model followed instructions for structural class and the number of coils and strands with near-perfect fidelity in three-dimensional designs. In a preliminary analysis of 30 motif-scaffolding challenges, where the model had to build a protein around a fixed arrangement of key amino acids, 43.7% of evaluated designs from its latest internal model met the structural success criteria, compared with 27.8% for RFdiffusion. ProteinMPNN supplied sequences and ESMFold predicted their folds for screening, so the rates reflect computational checks rather than laboratory demonstrations of function.

Recent findings suggest that openAI’s other evaluations produced varying margins over specialized systems. Across 200 challenges requiring a specified overall protein fold, 18.9% of evaluated designs from the latest internal model passed the computational criteria, compared with 17.1% for Proteina. In a small-molecule docking evaluation, predictions closely matched experimentally observed positions and orientations in 93% of scored GPT-6.2 cases and 96% of cases for the latest internal model, compared with 50% for DiffDock-L.

Sources indicate that whole-protein structure prediction remains the clearest weakness. OpenAI reports average TM-scores of 0.16 for GPT-5.6, 0.26 for GPT-6.2 and 0.38 for its latest internal model, compared with 0.93 for ESMFold2. A TM-score of 1 denotes a perfect structural match, while scores above 0.5 generally indicate that a prediction captures the overall fold.

The campaign also relied on Boltz-2, OpenDDE and ESMFold2 to filter candidates. The results therefore do not establish that GPT models can generate fresh minibinders end to end without specialized assistance. OpenAI cautioned that unusually strong inverse-folding results may partly reflect memorization or artifacts left by structure-generation processes, while public antibody-docking structures may have appeared in training or resembled training examples.

It has been revealed that binding is only an initial requirement for a useful research tool or medicine. Further work would need to establish specificity, stability and biological activity, along with safety and efficacy for therapeutic applications. OpenAI’s stated next steps include finding binders for harder targets, designing for biological effects, selectivity and manufacturability, expanding to RNA and small molecules, and evaluating biosecurity risks from possible misuse of the same capabilities.

The reported results position GPT-6 as a flexible design aid whose outputs still depend on specialized filtering and laboratory validation. Their practical value now rests on whether prompt-controlled candidates can consistently become selective, stable and biologically active molecules rather than merely bind their targets.
